api-design-pagination-versioning-and-err.title: Pagination, versioning and errors in API design
api-design-pagination-versioning-and-err.description: Offset and cursor pagination, which API changes break clients, how to evolve and deprecate safely, and how to report errors, conflicts and rate limits.

questions.text: A mobile app loads a busy feed with GET /posts?sort=-created_at&limit=20&offset=40. While the user reads that page, ten new posts are published. What does the app get when it then asks for offset=60?

options.text: Ten posts are skipped and the user never sees them
Ten posts from the previous page show up again, as every post moved down ten places
The same posts as before, because the database keeps a snapshot from the first page's query
An error, because the server notices that the data has changed since the first page was served

questions.explanation: An offset is only a position in the current ordering, so ten inserts at the top push every older post down ten places and the next page repeats ten posts from the previous one (deletions would cause skips instead). A cursor that names the last post seen, such as WHERE created_at < :last_seen, is not affected by what is inserted above it, and the database keeps no snapshot between separate requests.

questions.text: Which statements about cursor (keyset) pagination are correct?

options.text: The next page starts right after the last item seen, so items inserted above it neither shift the page nor repeat on it
The sort order needs a unique tie-breaker such as id; otherwise items that share a timestamp can be skipped or repeated at a page boundary
Clients can jump straight to page 50 as easily as they can with offsets
The same filters and sort order must be sent with every request that uses the cursor, because it only means something for the query that produced it
An exact total count becomes free, because the cursor carries it

questions.explanation: A cursor stores a position in a sorted, unique order (usually the last item's sort key), so with an index each page is a quick seek that inserts do not disturb; the tie-breaker keeps that order strictly defined, and the filters and sort must stay the same for the cursor to mean anything. The price is that you cannot jump to an arbitrary page, and a total count still needs its own query.

questions.text: Returning an opaque cursor token (or a ready-made 'next' link) instead of expecting clients to build the next request themselves lets the server change how paging works later without breaking clients.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: If clients only pass the token back untouched, its contents (a key, a timestamp, an encoded filter) are an implementation detail the server can change freely. Clients that decode or assemble cursors themselves start depending on that format, so the API can no longer change it; links the client simply follows are the light end of hypermedia (HATEOAS) for the same reason.

questions.text: Which changes to a live JSON API are safe for existing clients, assuming those clients ignore fields they do not recognise?

options.text: Adding a new optional field to a response
Renaming a response field from total to total_amount
Adding a new optional query parameter whose default keeps the old behaviour
Making a request field that used to be optional required
Adding a new endpoint

questions.explanation: Additive changes leave every request and response that already worked still working. A rename removes the name clients read, and a newly required request field breaks every client that does not send it yet; changing the type or meaning of a field is breaking in the same way.

questions.text: The team wants to rename the response field total to total_amount. What is the least disruptive way to do it?

options.text: Rename it now and describe the change in the release notes, because the new name is much clearer
Rename it now and raise the patch number, so clients can see that something changed
Return both fields, announce a removal date for total, and drop it after clients have moved
Publish a /v2 with the new name and switch /v1 off on the same day

questions.explanation: Expand, then contract: while both names exist nothing breaks, and an announced sunset date (for example in a Sunset header and the changelog) gives clients time to move. Renaming in place breaks every client that reads the old name, whatever number you bump; a new major version is for breaking changes you cannot avoid, and switching v1 off the same day only moves the break.

questions.text: An API follows JSON Merge Patch semantics for PATCH. A client sends PATCH /users/42 with the body {"nickname": null}. What should the server do?

options.text: Clear the stored nickname and leave every other field as it is
Ignore the field, because null carries no value
Reject the request, because null is not a valid value for any field
Replace the whole user with one whose only value is a null nickname

questions.explanation: In Merge Patch a field that is present is applied (null means remove or clear it) and a field that is absent is left alone, so the server must tell null from omission. Treating null as 'not sent' makes it impossible to clear a field, and treating the body as a full replacement would erase everything else, which is what PUT does.

questions.text: Which of these failures is best reported as 409 Conflict, rather than as a validation error such as 400 or 422?

options.text: The body leaves out the quantity field, which this endpoint requires in every request that is sent to it
The end date in the body is earlier than the start date that appears in the same body
The body is cut off halfway through, so it cannot be parsed as JSON at all
The room was booked by someone else a moment ago, so the request clashes with current state

questions.explanation: 400 and 422 mean the request itself is faulty (it cannot be parsed, or it parses but breaks a rule), so the fix is a different body. 409 means the request is fine in itself but clashes with the current state of the resource, such as a taken slot, a duplicate or an edit made by someone else, so it may succeed after the client re-reads the state. Many APIs use 400 for every validation failure; what matters most is using one convention consistently.

questions.text: Which error response is easiest for many different clients to handle correctly and consistently?

options.text: Status 500 for every failure, so clients need only one rule, with the real reason written in the body
The right 4xx or 5xx status plus one body shape everywhere: a stable code, a message and field details
A correct status code plus a carefully worded free-text message that clients read to decide what to do next
A tailor-made error shape for each endpoint, with each one described in that endpoint's documentation

questions.explanation: The status code tells caches, proxies and retry logic what class of failure happened, and a stable machine-readable code lets clients branch without parsing text, while the message stays free for humans and can be reworded or translated safely. One shape on every endpoint (for example application/problem+json) means each client needs only one error handler.

questions.text: A client sends more than its allowed 100 requests per minute. Which response is best?

options.text: 403 Forbidden, because the client is no longer allowed to call the API
503 Service Unavailable, because the server is too busy for this client
429 Too Many Requests, with a Retry-After header saying when to try again
200 OK with an empty result, so that well-behaved clients carry on without errors

questions.explanation: 429 tells the client it is sending too much, and Retry-After says when trying again makes sense, so a well-behaved client backs off instead of hammering the API. 403 suggests the access is withdrawn for good, 503 blames the server although the problem is this client's rate, and a fake 200 hides the problem. Many APIs also return headers such as X-RateLimit-Remaining so that clients can slow down before they hit the limit.

questions.text: When a client retries a POST /payments request after a timeout, it should send a freshly generated Idempotency-Key on every attempt, so that the server can tell the attempts apart.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The key identifies the operation, not the attempt: every retry of the same payment must reuse the same key, so the server recognises the repeat and returns the first result instead of charging again. A new key on each attempt makes every retry look like a brand-new payment.

azure-vnet-peering-and-private-endpoints.title: Azure VNet peering and private endpoints
azure-vnet-peering-and-private-endpoints.description: How peering connects VNets, why it is not transitive, and what a private endpoint needs before a service name resolves privately.

questions.text: Spoke A and spoke B are each peered with the same hub VNet, but not with each other. By default, can a VM in spoke A reach a VM in spoke B?

options.text: Yes, because both are peered to the hub, traffic flows through it automatically
Yes, but only if both spokes are in the same region
No, because peering is not transitive and connects only the two VNets directly peered
No, because a VNet can have only one peering

questions.explanation: Peering links two VNets directly and nothing more. To connect the spokes, peer them directly or route their traffic through a firewall or NVA in the hub. A VNet can have many peerings, which is what hub-and-spoke relies on.

questions.text: You created a peering from hub-vnet to spokeA-vnet and its state is Initiated, not Connected. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The matching peering from spokeA-vnet back to hub-vnet has not been created
Peering needs a VPN gateway in both VNets first
The hub needs a public IP address
Peerings take 24 hours to move to Connected

questions.explanation: A peering is two links, one created from each VNet's side, and it is Connected only when both exist and point at each other. Same-region peering needs no gateway, and no public IP is involved.

questions.text: You try to peer two VNets that both use the address space 10.0.0.0/16. What happens, and what is the remedy?

options.text: It works, and Azure automatically translates the overlapping addresses
It works if you add --allow-forwarded-traffic to both links
It fails; you can tell Azure which VNet owns the range with a route table
It fails; the only fix is to re-address one of the VNets

questions.explanation: Address spaces of peered VNets must not overlap, because Azure could not tell which network an address belongs to. There is no override or NAT that rescues it, so one VNet has to change its address space.

questions.text: How does a private endpoint for a storage account differ from a service endpoint?

options.text: A private endpoint gives the service a private IP in your subnet, so its public endpoint can be disabled; a service endpoint keeps the public IP and only routes to it privately
A private endpoint only works for storage accounts, while a service endpoint works for any VM
A private endpoint is free and a service endpoint is billed per hour
A private endpoint routes traffic over the public internet with extra encryption

questions.explanation: A private endpoint is a NIC with a private IP in your VNet mapped to one service instance, which removes the service from public exposure. A service endpoint still uses the service's public address. Private endpoints are billed hourly plus per GB, and they work across many PaaS services.

questions.text: You created a private endpoint for a storage account, but nslookup of myacct.blob.core.windows.net from a VM in the same VNet still returns a public IP. What is missing?

options.text: A second private endpoint in the same subnet
A private DNS zone named privatelink.blob.core.windows.net, linked to the VNet, with an A record for the endpoint
An NSG rule that allows UDP port 53
A peering to the VNet that holds the storage account

questions.explanation: The app still uses the public hostname, so something must make that name resolve to the private IP, which is what the linked privatelink zone and its A record do. Without it the endpoint exists but nothing uses it.

questions.text: You want spoke-to-spoke traffic to flow through a firewall in the hub. Which settings are needed? Select all that apply.

options.text: Allow forwarded traffic on the peerings
Route tables that send spoke traffic for the other spoke to the hub firewall
A public IP address on every VM in both spokes
--use-remote-gateways on each spoke peering, so that the firewall can forward traffic

questions.explanation: The peerings must accept traffic that was forwarded by the firewall and did not originate in the VNet it arrives from, and the spokes need routes that point at the firewall. Gateway transit is for sharing a VPN or ExpressRoute gateway, and nothing in this design needs public IPs.

questions.text: Traffic between two peered VNets travels over the public internet.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Peered VNets talk over Azure's private backbone using private IPs, and it never crosses the public internet. Same-region peering needs no gateway at all, which is a main reason to prefer peering over a VPN between VNets.

questions.text: A private endpoint lives in spokeA. A VM in the peered spokeB can reach the endpoint's private IP, but the storage name still resolves to the public IP from spokeB. What is the cause?

options.text: Peering does not carry traffic to private endpoints
The privatelink private DNS zone is linked only to spokeA, and spokeB needs a link too
The private endpoint must be recreated in spokeB
The storage account must be moved to spokeB's subnet

questions.explanation: Peering carries the traffic, but name resolution comes from private DNS zones linked to a VNet. A VM only sees the zone's records if its VNet is linked (or shares a resolver that can see them), so both parts are needed.

big-o-and-data-structures.title: Big-O and data structures
big-o-and-data-structures.description: What common operations on lists, dicts, sets, heaps and deques cost, and how to spot the code that quietly turns quadratic.

questions.text: A loop handles n incoming orders. For each one it checks if order_id in seen_ids, where seen_ids is a Python list that grows as new ids are appended. What is the total running time?

options.text: O(n), because the loop body runs once per order and each step is a single check
O(log n), because Python uses binary search when you test membership in a list
O(n^2), because each in check scans the list, and the list keeps growing
O(n log n), because each in check sorts the list before looking for the id

questions.explanation: A membership test on a list compares the id with the items one by one, so each check costs O(n) and n checks add up to O(n^2). Keeping the seen ids in a set makes each check O(1) on average and the whole loop O(n), at the price of extra memory for the set. Counting only the outer loop, as the first option does, ignores the work inside each check.

questions.text: How can a Python dict find a key in O(1) time on average, and what makes it slower in the worst case?

options.text: It keeps its keys sorted and binary-searches them; the worst case is keys that arrive out of order
It hashes the key to jump near its slot; many keys colliding on the same slots slows it down
It checks the newest entries first; the worst case is a key that was added long ago
It caches the result of every lookup it has seen; the worst case is a key it has never been asked for

questions.explanation: The key's hash tells the dict (and a set, which works the same way) roughly where its entry lives, so a lookup inspects one slot or a few instead of scanning everything. If many keys collide on the same slots, because of a poor hash function or hostile input, lookups degrade towards O(n). Dicts are not sorted, and they do not cache lookups.

questions.text: Appending to a Python list is called amortised O(1). What does amortised mean here?

options.text: Every single append takes exactly the same constant time, however full the list is
Append is constant time only while the list is kept sorted, and slower otherwise
The list reserves memory for all the data it will ever hold when it is created
Occasional resizes are expensive, but averaged over many appends the cost is constant

questions.explanation: When a list runs out of spare room, Python allocates a larger block and copies every item, an O(n) step. Because each new block leaves room for many more appends, such copies are rare and the average cost per append stays constant, although a single append can occasionally be slow.

questions.text: A program adds jobs at the back of a queue and takes them from the front, millions of times. Which choice keeps both operations cheap?

options.text: A collections.deque, which adds and removes at either end in O(1)
A list, using append() to add a job and pop(0) to take the next one
A list, using insert(0, job) to add a job and pop() to take the next one
A set, because adding and removing a member is O(1) on average

questions.explanation: A deque is built for fast work at both ends, so append and popleft are O(1). On a list, pop(0) and insert(0, x) have to shift every other item, so each costs O(n) and millions of them become very slow. A set has no order, so it cannot say which job came first.

questions.text: You are reading a stream of 10 million numbers and want only the 10 largest, without keeping them all in memory. What is the best approach?

options.text: Sort all 10 million numbers, then slice off the last 10 of them
Load every number into a max-heap, then pop the largest item 10 times, one after another
A min-heap of size 10: replace its smallest item whenever a bigger number arrives
Store every number in a set, then take the maximum of the set 10 times

questions.explanation: A min-heap capped at 10 items needs only a little memory, and each number costs at most one heap operation on 10 items, so the pass takes O(n log k) time with k = 10 (heapq.nlargest does exactly this). Sorting, or a max-heap or set of everything, takes O(n) memory, which the problem rules out.

questions.text: You keep a Python list sorted by calling bisect.insort(items, x) for every new item. Roughly what does one insert cost, for a list of n items?

options.text: O(1), because bisect jumps straight to the right position in the list
O(log n), because binary search finds the position and that is all the work
O(n log n), because insort sorts the whole list again after each insert
O(n): the search is O(log n), but later items must shift to make room

questions.explanation: bisect finds the insertion point in O(log n) comparisons, but a Python list is an array, so every item after that point has to move along one place, which is O(n). A sorted list with bisect suits data that is searched often and changed rarely; for frequent inserts, a heap (if you only need the smallest item) or a tree-based structure fits better.

questions.text: Which of these patterns can make a program take roughly O(n^2) time as n grows?

options.text: Two nested loops that each go over the whole list of n items
One loop that appends each of n items to a list
A loop that calls my_list.remove(item) once per item on a list of n items
A loop that counts n words with counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1
A loop that builds a long string with result += piece when each += copies everything built so far

questions.explanation: Nested loops multiply their work, list.remove has to search and then shift the list, and repeatedly copying a growing string adds up the same way, so each of those is O(n^2) over n steps. Appending to a list and updating a dict entry are O(1) on average, so those loops stay O(n).

questions.text: Which statements about memory use (space complexity) are true?

options.text: A dict that gives O(1) lookups also uses only O(1) memory
A set built from n ids needs memory proportional to n, even though each lookup is O(1) on average
sorted(items) sorts in place, so it needs no extra memory for the result
A recursive function that goes n calls deep needs O(n) memory for its call stack
A generator that yields one line of a large file at a time keeps only a small, constant amount of data in memory

questions.explanation: Fast lookups are not free in memory: a dict or set stores all n entries, so it takes O(n) space. Every pending call keeps a stack frame, so n-deep recursion costs O(n), while a generator holds just the current item. sorted() builds a new list of n items, whereas list.sort() reorders the existing one.

questions.text: To find a single value in an unsorted list, sorting the list first and then using binary search is faster than one linear scan.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Sorting costs O(n log n), which is more than the O(n) of a single scan, so sorting just to search once is slower. It pays off only when you search many times: you sort once, and each later lookup costs O(log n).

questions.text: Big-O describes how an algorithm's cost grows with the input size, so an O(n log n) algorithm can still be faster than an O(n) one on small inputs.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Big-O hides constant factors and says nothing about any one input size, so it tells you which approach wins as n grows, not which is quicker at a given n. On small inputs a simpler algorithm with a worse growth rate can win, which is why measuring still matters.

caching-strategies-and-eviction.title: Caching strategies and eviction
caching-strategies-and-eviction.description: Cache-aside, read-through, write-through and write-behind, plus eviction policies, TTLs and invalidation.

questions.text: What is the real difference between cache-aside and read-through?

options.text: Cache-aside never touches the database; read-through always does
Read-through lazy-loads on a miss; cache-aside preloads every key at startup
Cache-aside writes to the database first; read-through writes to the cache first
In cache-aside the application runs the miss logic; in read-through the cache layer loads from the source itself

questions.explanation: Both load lazily on a miss. The difference is organizational: who is responsible for fetching from the source and storing the result. Neither is about write order.

questions.text: In a cache-aside setup, a record is updated in the database. Which cache action is usually the safer default?

options.text: Delete the key so the next read reloads from the database
Overwrite the key with the new value
Leave the key alone and rely on LRU to remove it
Flush the entire cache

questions.explanation: Deleting makes the database the single source for the refreshed value. Overwriting reintroduces a race where two concurrent writers can leave the older value cached, and eviction does not fix a stale entry.

questions.text: A page-view counter is incremented in Redis and flushed to the database once a minute. What is the main risk of this write-behind design?

options.text: Reads of the counter become slower
Increments not yet flushed are lost if the cache fails
The database receives far more writes than before
The cache fills with keys nobody reads

questions.explanation: The write is acknowledged before it reaches durable storage, so a crash loses the unflushed window. That is acceptable for view counts and unacceptable for payments. Option c is the opposite of what happens: write-behind coalesces many writes into few.

questions.text: Write-through gives faster writes than cache-aside, because the cache absorbs the write.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Write-through acknowledges only after the database write and the cache write both finish, so the cache does not absorb anything: the write is no faster than cache-aside and pays for the extra cache write. Its benefit is that a read right after a write finds fresh data in the cache. The faster-write claim describes write-behind.

questions.text: A cache holds 3 entries and key A is read constantly. A nightly job then reads thousands of other keys once each. Which policy best protects A from being evicted?

options.text: LRU, because A was used recently at some point
FIFO, because A has been resident longest
LFU, because A's high access count outweighs the one-time scan keys
Random eviction, because it ignores how recently or how often a key was used

questions.explanation: A long scan makes A the least recently used, so LRU evicts it (cache pollution). LFU keeps it because of its count. FIFO evicts whatever has been resident longest, so it would push A out as soon as the scan fills the cache, and random eviction can drop A at any time because it ignores usage.

questions.text: Redis is used purely as a cache with maxmemory-policy volatile-lru, but the application never sets a TTL on its keys. What happens when memory is full?

options.text: The least recently used keys are evicted as usual
Redis picks random keys to evict
Redis restarts and drops all data
Nothing is eligible for eviction, so Redis starts rejecting writes with an out-of-memory error

questions.explanation: volatile-* policies only consider keys that have a TTL. With none, the cache behaves like noeviction. Use an allkeys-* policy for a pure cache, or set a TTL on every cache key.

questions.text: Which statements about cache invalidation are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: A TTL is worth keeping as a backstop even when you also invalidate explicitly
Event-based invalidation lets a writer bust caches it knows nothing about
Manual invalidation in application code stays correct when other services write to the database directly
A shorter TTL always lowers the load on the database

questions.explanation: A TTL bounds the damage of a missed invalidation, and an event subscriber decouples the writer from the caches. Manual deletes only cover the write paths you instrumented, and a shorter TTL means more misses and so more database load.

questions.text: A category rename should make thousands of cached list keys such as products:category:5:v3 stale, and you cannot enumerate them. What is a practical technique?

options.text: Run KEYS * and delete everything on each rename
Switch the cache to write-behind
Bump the version number embedded in the keys so the old keys are never read again and age out
Raise maxmemory so the stale entries do not matter

questions.explanation: Generational (version-based) invalidation makes the old keys unreachable at once with a single increment, and TTL or eviction cleans them up later. KEYS * walks every key in one blocking command (SCAN avoids the blocking but is still a full walk), and extra memory does not make stale data correct.

cap-and-consistency-models.title: CAP theorem and consistency models
cap-and-consistency-models.description: What CAP really forces you to choose, how it differs from ACID, and which consistency model each kind of feature needs.

questions.text: When does the CAP theorem force you to give up either consistency or availability?

options.text: Only while a network partition is happening
Always, on every request
Only when the system has more than three nodes
Only when the database uses SQL

questions.explanation: In normal operation a well-designed system offers both consistency and availability. The forced choice appears when nodes cannot reach each other and a request arrives.

questions.text: A system spread over several machines can choose to give up partition tolerance and so be both consistent and available.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Networks do drop and delay messages, so partitions will happen whether or not you plan for them. The real choice is what you do during one: refuse requests (CP) or serve possibly stale data (AP).

questions.text: During a partition, the minority side of a CP system receives a write. What does it do?

options.text: Accepts the write locally and reconciles later
Returns an error or blocks rather than risk inconsistency
Accepts the write and silently drops it later
Switches to eventual consistency until the partition heals

questions.explanation: CP means sacrificing availability on the side that cannot confirm it has the latest data. Option a describes an AP system.

questions.text: How does the C in CAP differ from the C in ACID?

options.text: They are the same guarantee under two names
CAP's C means a read sees the most recent completed write (linearizability); ACID's C means a transaction keeps the database within its rules
CAP's C is about durability on disk; ACID's C is about network delivery
ACID's C applies to distributed systems and CAP's C applies to single servers

questions.explanation: ACID consistency is about honoring constraints and invariants. A node can satisfy that while a replica still serves a valid but stale row, which violates CAP's consistency.

questions.text: Which consistency model guarantees that nobody sees a reply to a comment before the comment itself, without forcing one global order on unrelated events?

options.text: Eventual consistency
Strong consistency (linearizability)
Causal consistency
Read-your-writes consistency

questions.explanation: Causal consistency keeps related operations in the same order for everyone while leaving unrelated ones free. It is stronger than eventual and cheaper than linearizability. Read-your-writes only promises that you see your own writes.

questions.text: Which of these operations generally justify the cost of strong consistency? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reading an account balance just before approving a withdrawal
Showing a post's like count
Checking whether a username is already taken at signup
Refreshing an analytics dashboard

questions.explanation: A stale answer in a and c leads to a wrong decision with real consequences, such as an overdraft or a duplicate username. A few seconds of staleness in a like count or a dashboard is harmless, so paying for coordination there only adds latency.

questions.text: According to PACELC, what trade-off exists even when the network is healthy?

options.text: Between availability and partition tolerance
Between latency and consistency
Between throughput and durability only
There is no trade-off when there is no partition

questions.explanation: The Else clause: giving strong consistency means waiting for enough replicas to acknowledge, which costs round trips on every request. Relaxing consistency returns sooner. CAP alone says nothing about this normal-case cost, which is why option d is a misreading.

questions.text: A Dynamo-style store keeps N=3 replicas of each key and uses strict quorums. Which write and read quorum sizes guarantee that every read set overlaps the replicas that acknowledged the latest successful write?
questions.explanation: Overlap needs W + R > N, and 2 + 2 = 4 > 3. With W=2, R=1 or W=1, R=2 the sum is only 3, so a read can land entirely on replicas that missed the write. Overlap means at least one replica you read from has the write (the client still has to pick the newest version). Lower quorums are faster and more available, but only eventually consistent.

capacity-estimation-back-of-envelope.title: Capacity estimation and back-of-envelope math
capacity-estimation-back-of-envelope.description: Turn users into QPS, storage, bandwidth, server counts and cache size, and sanity-check the order of magnitude.

questions.text: Which constant is the most useful for turning a per-day count into a per-second rate in a quick estimate?

options.text: About 100,000 seconds per day (86,400, rounded to 10^5)
3,600 seconds per day
About 1,000,000 seconds per day
About 10,000 seconds per day

questions.explanation: There are 86,400 seconds in a day, so 10^5 is the clean round number and one division converts a daily total to an average rate. 3,600 is the number of seconds in an hour, a very common slip.

questions.text: A service has 50 million daily active users, and each makes 20 requests a day. Using the 10^5 seconds-per-day rule and a 3x peak factor, what is the peak request rate?

options.text: About 3,000 requests per second
About 10,000 requests per second
About 30,000 requests per second
About 300,000 requests per second

questions.explanation: 50M x 20 = 10^9 requests a day; divided by 10^5 that is about 10,000 per second on average, and times 3 is about 30,000 at peak. 10,000 is the average, which is the wrong number to size for.

questions.text: A service stores 10 million new records a day, each about 2 KB, and keeps them for one year with 3 copies. About how much storage does it need?

options.text: About 7.3 TB
About 220 TB
About 2.2 TB
About 22 TB

questions.explanation: 10M x 2 KB = 20 GB per day; x 365 is about 7.3 TB; x 3 copies is about 22 TB. The 7.3 TB answer forgets replication, which the real storage bill always includes.

questions.text: An API serves 20,000 requests per second with an average response of 50 KB. How much outbound bandwidth is that?

options.text: About 1 MB/s
About 100 MB/s (under 1 Gbps)
About 1 GB/s (about 8 Gbps)
About 10 GB/s (about 80 Gbps)

questions.explanation: Bandwidth is request rate times payload: 20,000 x 50 KB = 1,000,000 KB/s, which is 1 GB/s, or about 8 Gbps. That is more than a 1 Gbps network card can carry and most of a 10 Gbps one, which is the signal to spread the load or use a CDN.

questions.text: Peak load is 90,000 requests per second and one server sustains 15,000. How many servers do you provision if you add N+2 redundancy?
questions.explanation: 90,000 / 15,000 = 6 servers for load alone, plus 2 spare for failures and deploys gives 8. Six would run at exactly 100% of peak with nothing to lose, and doubling to 12 is more than N+2 asks for.

questions.text: Using the latency ladder (memory ~100 ns, SSD random read ~100 microseconds, disk seek ~10 ms, same-datacenter round trip ~0.5 ms, cross-continent round trip ~100+ ms), which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: A rotational disk seek is about as fast as an SSD random read
A main-memory reference is roughly 1,000 times faster than an SSD random read
A same-datacenter round trip is faster than a main-memory reference
One cross-continent round trip costs more than a million memory references

questions.explanation: 100 ns against 100 microseconds is 1,000x, and 100 ms against 100 ns is about 10^6x. A disk seek is roughly 100x slower than an SSD read, and any network round trip is far slower than touching memory.

questions.text: A chat service sends 2 billion messages a day. Dividing by 3,600 gives the right average messages per second.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: 3,600 is the number of seconds in an hour. Dividing by about 10^5 gives roughly 20,000 messages per second on average, more than 20 times lower than the roughly 555,000 per second that dividing by 3,600 gives, and you still apply a peak factor on top.

questions.text: An app touches 100 TB of distinct data a day, and requests follow the 80/20 rule. You cache the hot 20% on nodes with 256 GB of RAM each. Roughly how many nodes are needed?

options.text: About 8
About 80
About 800

questions.explanation: 20% of 100 TB is 20 TB, and 20,000 GB / 256 GB is about 78, so roughly 80 nodes. The number shows that one Redis node is not enough and a distributed cache is required.

ci-cd-and-deployment-strategies.title: CI/CD and deployment strategies
ci-cd-and-deployment-strategies.description: What continuous integration, delivery and deployment mean, how pipelines fail fast, how rolling, blue/green and canary releases trade risk for cost, and how to roll back safely with a database.

questions.text: A team's pipeline builds every merged change, runs all the tests and deploys the build to a staging environment. A person then presses a button to send a chosen build to production. Which practice is this?

options.text: Continuous integration, which is everything up to the point where merged code has been built and tested
Continuous deployment, because every change reaches an environment without manual work
Continuous delivery: every change stays ready to release, and a person decides when it goes live
Trunk-based development, because all merged changes go through one pipeline

questions.explanation: Continuous integration merges and tests every change automatically; continuous delivery goes further by keeping every change in a releasable state, with a human decision for the production release; continuous deployment removes that last manual step and ships every change that passes. The button is the human decision, so this is delivery, not deployment.

questions.text: A pipeline runs a 40-minute end-to-end suite first, then 2 minutes of unit tests, then 30 seconds of lint. A typo that breaks the lint step is reported only after 43 minutes. What does the fail-fast principle suggest?

options.text: Put cheap, fast checks first and slow ones last, so most failures show up in seconds
Put the most thorough test first, because it gives the most valuable feedback
Drop the cheap checks entirely, because the end-to-end suite already covers everything they check
Use any order, because the total time is the same whichever stage happens to fail

questions.explanation: Fail fast means putting the cheapest, most-likely-to-fail checks (formatting, lint, unit tests) first, so a broken change is rejected in seconds and the expensive stages never run for it. Order does matter for failing builds: with the thorough test first, every typo costs 40 minutes of runner time and developer waiting, even though a passing build takes the same total time either way.

questions.text: A team wants to expose a risky change to about 5% of real traffic, watch error rates and latency, and widen the rollout only if the numbers stay healthy. Which deployment strategy fits?

options.text: A rolling update, which replaces instances batch by batch until all run the new version
Blue/green, which builds a second full environment and switches all traffic over to it at once
Recreate, which stops every instance of the old version and then starts the new one
A canary release, which sends a small slice of traffic to the new version and compares it

questions.explanation: A canary sends a small share of real traffic to the new version and compares its error rate and latency with the old one, so a bad release hurts only that slice and is quickly reversed. A rolling update keeps replacing instances on a schedule without comparing versions, blue/green moves all traffic at once, and recreate means downtime.

questions.text: Which statements about deployment strategies are correct?

options.text: During a rolling update, old and new versions serve traffic at the same time, so the two must be able to work side by side
Blue/green keeps the previous version running, so rolling back can be as quick as switching traffic back
Blue/green needs no extra capacity, because only one environment runs at a time
A canary release depends on good metrics and alerts, because its whole point is comparing the new version with the old on real traffic
A rolling update keeps the old instances running aside, so going back to the old version is instant

questions.explanation: Rolling and canary releases mix versions in production for a while, so the versions must coexist; blue/green buys a quick switch back by running two full environments; and a canary is only as good as the metrics used to judge it. A rolling update replaces instances in place, so going back means another rolling update rather than one switch of traffic.

questions.text: A team wants to merge an unfinished checkout redesign into the main branch and deploy it to production often, without customers seeing it until it is ready. What is the usual technique?

options.text: Keep the redesign on a long-lived branch of its own and merge it only on release day
Hide the new code path behind a feature flag that stays off until the team switches it on
Deploy it to a separate, second production environment whose address only the staff members know about
Deploy only at night or at weekends, when few customers are online to notice

questions.explanation: A feature flag separates deploy (the code is on the production servers) from release (users get the feature), so unfinished work can be merged in small steps, shipped dark, enabled for staff or a percentage of users, and switched off again without a redeploy. A long-lived branch postpones integration and makes the final merge risky, and deploying at night hides nothing from the customers who are online. Remove flags once the feature is fully rolled out.

questions.text: A pipeline compiles the code again from the same commit for staging and then for production. Staging passes, but production behaves differently and no one can reproduce it. Which practice would have prevented this?

options.text: Run the same build commands in every environment, because identical commands always give identical output
Tag each build latest, so that every environment pulls the same name
Build once into an immutable artifact, such as an image pinned by digest, and promote that same artifact
Keep one long-lived branch per environment and merge changes upward from staging

questions.explanation: Rebuilding per environment means what you tested is not what you ship: dependency versions, base images and build timestamps can differ even for the same commit. Build once, then promote the same artifact through staging to production and vary only the configuration. A latest tag is mutable, so it can point to different bits at different times.

questions.text: A release drops the column middle_name and deploys code that no longer uses it, in a single step. The release has a bug, the team rolls back the code, and the old version now crashes. What would have made the rollback safe?

options.text: Take a database backup before every release and restore it whenever a rollback is needed
Split it up: first ship code that stops using the column, and drop the column in a later release
Write a down migration that re-adds the column, and run it as part of every rollback, so the schema matches the code
Run the same migration after the new code is fully deployed instead of before it, within the same release

questions.explanation: A rollback puts the old code in front of the new schema, whenever the migration ran, so every schema change has to work with both versions. Expand and contract does this in steps: add what is new, move the code over, and remove what is old only in a later release. Restoring a backup loses everything written since the release, and re-adding a dropped column cannot bring its data back.

questions.text: During a rolling update, a new instance can safely receive traffic as soon as its process has started, so a readiness check only slows the deployment down.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: A started process is not necessarily ready: it may still be warming caches, opening database connections or running startup tasks. A readiness check keeps traffic away until the instance can really serve requests, and a rollout that waits for it halts instead of replacing healthy instances with broken ones.

questions.text: Which practices keep secrets safe in a CI/CD pipeline?

options.text: Store them in the CI system's secret store or a vault, and give each job only the secrets it needs
Commit them to the repository, because a private repository keeps them safe
Prefer short-lived credentials issued to the pipeline at run time, for example through OIDC federation, over long-lived keys
Run jobs for pull requests from forks with the production secrets, so that their tests behave like production
Scan commits and build output for leaked secrets, and rotate any that turn up

questions.explanation: A secret committed to a repository is copied to every clone and stays in the history even after deletion, private or not, while a secret store with narrow scoping, short-lived credentials, and scanning with rotation limit both the exposure and the value of a leak. Code from forks is untrusted and could print or send every secret the job can see.

questions.text: In trunk-based development, developers merge small changes into the main branch often (typically at least daily) and hide unfinished work behind feature flags instead of keeping it on long-lived branches.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Frequent small merges surface conflicts and incompatibilities within hours rather than weeks, which is what continuous integration is for, and flags keep half-finished features invisible to users. Long-lived branches postpone that integration and make the eventual merge risky.

concurrency-async-and-race-conditions.title: Concurrency, async and race conditions
concurrency-async-and-race-conditions.description: Processes, threads and async tasks, how races and deadlocks happen, and what keeps shared state correct: locks, atomic operations and optimistic checks.

questions.text: A chat server must keep 10,000 WebSocket connections open at once, and almost all of them are idle at any moment. Which concurrency model fits best?

options.text: One process per connection, so that a crash only affects one user
One OS thread per connection, each blocked while it waits on its own socket
Async tasks on an event loop, each resumed only when its connection is ready
A single thread that checks each connection in turn and blocks until data arrives on it

questions.explanation: Idle connections spend nearly all their time waiting, so cheap async tasks win: a task is little more than a small object, while an OS thread needs its own stack and scheduler time and a process far more. One thread per connection works for a few thousand but gets costly, and blocking on one connection at a time lets a single silent client stall all the others.

questions.text: Calling three independent APIs one after another takes about 900 ms, because each answers in about 300 ms and merging the results is instant. Starting all three at once with async I/O takes about 300 ms, even on one CPU core. Why?

options.text: Async I/O spreads the three calls over three CPU cores, so they genuinely run in parallel
It is all waiting, not computing, so one thread can start all three and resume each as its reply arrives
Async I/O makes every individual call about three times faster, so the total drops by the same factor
The runtime merges the three calls into one network request, so the three round trips become a single one

questions.explanation: The 900 ms is almost entirely waiting for the network, and waiting needs no CPU, so one event loop can start all three requests and continue each when its reply arrives. Each call still takes 300 ms, and the trick would not help CPU-bound work such as hashing or compressing, where the cores are the limit.

questions.text: A server built on a single-threaded event loop (such as Node.js or Python's asyncio) is serving many requests. One handler calls a synchronous, CPU-heavy function that runs for 3 seconds. What happens to the other requests meanwhile?

options.text: They are handled on other threads of the same process, so only the one slow request is affected
The operating system moves them to idle CPU cores, so the server keeps serving them as usual
Only requests for the same endpoint are delayed, because the loop schedules each route separately
They all wait, because the loop cannot run anything else until the handler gives control back

questions.explanation: Async code is cooperative: the loop switches tasks only when one awaits something, and a long synchronous call never gives control back, so every other request, even a health check, stalls. Move CPU-heavy work to a worker pool of threads or processes, or split it into awaitable pieces.

questions.text: In a single-threaded async service, a handler runs two steps: balance = await db.get_balance(account), then await db.set_balance(account, balance - 10). Two requests for the same account run at the same moment. Can one of the two withdrawals be lost?

options.text: Yes: each await lets the other request run, so both can read the same balance before either writes it back
No: a single thread runs one request from start to finish before it starts the next
No: the event loop runs awaited database calls strictly in the order they were issued, so they cannot overlap
Yes, but only if the service also runs as several processes

questions.explanation: Async tasks interleave at every await, so a single thread does not mean one request at a time: both requests can read the same balance and both write balance - 10, losing one withdrawal. Make the change one atomic statement (SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE balance >= 10), or hold a lock or check a version across the whole read-then-write; more processes only add more ways to interleave.

questions.text: Two requests run the same code at the same moment against shared state. Which of these sequences can go wrong?

options.text: Read the stock level, check that it is above zero, then write stock - 1, as three separate steps in application code
Run UPDATE items SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 7 AND stock > 0, then check how many rows it changed
Look up an email address and insert a new user if none was found, with no unique constraint on the email column
Read a settings value that is loaded once at startup and never modified
Increase a shared in-memory counter from several threads with count = count + 1 and no lock

questions.explanation: In a, c and e there is a gap between reading or checking and writing, so both requests can pass the check or start from the same value (check-then-act and read-modify-write races). In b the database does the check and the change as one atomic statement, and d is safe because nothing ever writes to the data.

questions.text: Two instances of the same service, running on different servers, can race on the same database row, and a mutex inside each instance's code does not prevent it.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: A mutex lives in one process's memory, so an instance on another machine never sees it. State shared between instances needs protection that the shared store (or a shared lock service) enforces: a unique constraint, an atomic UPDATE, a row lock inside a transaction, or a version check.

questions.text: Two code paths each need both lock A and lock B, and they sometimes deadlock. Which changes would make a deadlock between them impossible?

options.text: Make every code path take the locks in the same order, always A before B
Take A, then try B without waiting; if B is busy, release A and retry after a short random pause
Run the code paths on a larger thread pool, so that there are more threads to wait on
Shorten the critical sections, so that the two paths rarely hold the locks at the same time
Make the locks re-entrant, so that a thread can take a lock it already holds

questions.explanation: A deadlock needs four things at once: exclusive locks, hold-and-wait, no way to take a lock away, and a circular wait. A global lock order removes the circular wait, and releasing what you hold when the next lock is busy removes hold-and-wait. More threads, shorter sections and re-entrancy only change how often the problem shows up or what one thread can do alone.

questions.text: Hundreds of requests per second try to decrement the stock of one flash-sale item. The code reads the row's stock and version, then updates it with WHERE version equal to the version it read, and retries when no row matched. Why does this optimistic approach struggle here?

options.text: Every update has to wait for a lock held by the writers ahead of it in line
The version check only works when the version column has its own index, which a hot row lacks
Most attempts find the version already changed, so they fail and retry, wasting work
A version column cannot tell apart two writers whose updates arrive within the same millisecond

questions.explanation: Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are rare: nobody waits, and a stale write is detected and retried. On a hot row almost every attempt conflicts, so most of the work is thrown away and some requests may keep losing; let the database serialize those writers instead, ideally with one atomic UPDATE items SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock > 0.

questions.text: Requests are handed to a fixed pool of worker threads through a queue. A traffic spike fills the queue and the workers cannot keep up. Which response keeps the service healthiest?

options.text: Let the queue grow as large as it needs to, so that no request is ever turned away, however long it has to wait
Cap the queue and refuse new work fast (for example with a 503) so queued work still finishes on time
Raise the pool to thousands of threads so that the backlog clears faster than before the spike
Let every request wait with no timeout, because each one will be served in the end eventually

questions.explanation: A bounded queue gives back-pressure: when it is full, new work is refused or slowed, so memory use and waiting time stay limited and clients can back off and retry. An unbounded queue turns overload into ever longer waits and finally out-of-memory, and thousands of threads mostly add context switching and competition for the same CPUs and database connections.

questions.text: A payment endpoint looks up the client's idempotency key and, only if it is not found, charges the card and then saves the key with the result. This guarantees the card is charged once, even when two retries of the same request arrive at the same moment.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Both retries can run the lookup before either has saved the key, so both find nothing and both charge the card; the lookup and the save are a check-then-act race. Claim the key first with an atomic insert under a unique constraint (or take a lock on the key), and let the loser wait for the stored result or answer 409.

cors-csrf-and-xss.title: CORS, CSRF and XSS
cors-csrf-and-xss.description: What the same-origin policy and CORS protect, and how to defend against forged requests, injected scripts and clickjacking.

questions.text: Which of these URLs have the same origin as https://shop.example.com/cart?

options.text: https://shop.example.com/account/orders
http://shop.example.com/cart
https://api.example.com/cart
https://shop.example.com:443/help
https://shop.example.com:8443/cart

questions.explanation: An origin is the combination of scheme, host and port; the path does not matter. Port 443 is the default for https, so spelling it out changes nothing, while a different scheme, a different subdomain or a different port makes a different origin.

questions.text: If an API sends CORS headers that allow only https://app.example.com, programs such as curl or a server-side script can no longer call it.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: CORS is a rule that browsers apply to web pages: it decides whether a page from another origin may read a response. curl and other servers do not enforce it, so the API still needs authentication and authorization on every request.

questions.text: JavaScript on https://app.example.com sends fetch with the method PUT and a JSON body to https://api.example.com. What does the browser do first?

options.text: It sends an OPTIONS preflight first and sends the PUT only if the answer allows it
It sends the PUT straight away and checks the CORS headers when the response arrives
It refuses to send any cross-origin PUT request, whatever the other server says
It shows the user a prompt asking for permission to contact the other site

questions.explanation: A cross-origin request that is not simple, such as a PUT or one with a JSON content type or an Authorization header, triggers a preflight OPTIONS request in which the server states which origins, methods and headers it accepts. Simple requests, like a basic GET or a form-style POST, skip it and are sent at once, which is also why CORS alone does not stop CSRF.

questions.text: An API copies whatever Origin header it receives into Access-Control-Allow-Origin and also sends Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. What is the problem?

options.text: Browsers reject the response, because those two headers may never be used together
Attackers can log in without a valid session, because the API no longer checks any credentials
Any website can have a visitor's browser call the API with their cookies and read the data
Only simple GET requests are affected, because preflighted requests simply ignore these headers

questions.explanation: The server is telling browsers that every origin may read credentialed responses, so a malicious page can fetch a visitor's private data using their own cookies. A wildcard * with credentials is refused by browsers, which is why people reflect the origin instead; the fix is a fixed allowlist of trusted origins. Authentication is not bypassed; the attacker borrows the victim's session.

questions.text: A banking site keeps users signed in with a session cookie. A hidden form on a malicious page submits a POST to the bank's transfer endpoint. Why can that work, and what stops it?

options.text: The page reads the cookie with JavaScript and copies it, so the cookie should be marked HttpOnly
Browsers attach the bank's cookie to any request to the bank; use SameSite and a CSRF token
The form travels over plain HTTP where anyone can read it, so the endpoint must use HTTPS
CORS lets the other site read the bank's response, so the CORS headers should be removed

questions.explanation: CSRF abuses the fact that cookies are attached automatically, so the forged request arrives with the victim's real session. SameSite cookies stop browsers sending the cookie on most cross-site requests, and a secret CSRF token that the attacker cannot read makes the request impossible to forge. HttpOnly guards against scripts reading the cookie, which is a different attack, and the forged request never needs to read the response.

questions.text: A forum saves each post in its database and shows it to every reader without encoding it. An attacker posts a script tag, and it runs in every reader's browser. What is this, and what is the root fix?

options.text: Reflected XSS; stop using GET requests for the forum's search page
DOM-based XSS; set the HttpOnly flag on the forum's session cookie
Stored XSS; delete script tags from posts when they are saved
Stored XSS; encode each post for HTML when it is displayed

questions.explanation: Stored XSS keeps the payload on the server and hits every visitor who views it, unlike reflected XSS (echoed back from one request) or DOM-based XSS (created by script running in the browser). The root fix is to encode data for the place it is written, such as HTML text; deleting script tags on the way in is easy to bypass with other tags and event attributes, and does nothing for data already stored.

questions.text: Which of these are safe ways to show untrusted text, such as a value from the URL or from an API, in a web page?

options.text: Assign it with element.textContent
Assign it with element.innerHTML after removing any script tags
Render it through a template engine or UI framework that escapes values by default
Build an inline onclick attribute from it after removing double quotes

questions.explanation: textContent and auto-escaping templates treat the value as plain text, never as markup. innerHTML parses it as HTML, and removing script tags does not help because other elements, such as an img with an onerror handler, also run code. Gluing a value into an inline event handler after stripping quotes fails for the same reason: you are still building code out of data.

questions.text: A page is served with Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self'. An attacker manages to inject an inline script tag into it. What does the browser do?

options.text: It runs it, because the page that contains the script was served from the same origin
It blocks it, because inline scripts are refused unless the policy allows them
It runs it, but stops it from reading cookies or other stored data
It blocks it only after the server has confirmed that the script is really malicious

questions.explanation: script-src 'self' tells the browser to run only scripts loaded from your own origin, and inline script blocks are refused unless the policy opts in, for example with unsafe-inline or a nonce. CSP limits what injected markup can do, but it is a second line of defence: you still need output encoding to remove the bug itself.

questions.text: If a session cookie is marked HttpOnly, a cross-site scripting bug can no longer be used to act as the logged-in user.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: HttpOnly stops scripts from reading the cookie, so it cannot be copied away, but injected script still runs inside the victim's logged-in page and can send requests that carry the cookie automatically. It limits the damage of XSS; it does not remove the need to fix it.

questions.text: An attacker loads your 'Delete account' page in a transparent iframe on their own site and tricks visitors into clicking its button. Which response header tells browsers not to display your pages inside other sites' frames?

options.text: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://example.com
Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self'

questions.explanation: frame-ancestors lists the origins that may embed the page, and 'none' or 'self' stops other sites from framing it, so a hidden overlay cannot trick users into clicking. The older X-Frame-Options header does a similar job. HSTS, nosniff and the CORS headers control HTTPS use, content-type guessing and cross-origin reads, not framing.

database-indexes.title: Database indexes
database-indexes.description: What an index buys, what it costs, and how to tell whether a query is using one.

questions.text: What does an index mainly speed up?

options.text: Inserts
Reads that filter or sort on the indexed columns
Table creation
Backups

questions.explanation: An index is an ordered structure the database can search instead of scanning the whole table.

questions.text: Adding more B-tree indexes to a table generally makes its inserts, updates and deletes slower.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: A write usually has to update each index that covers the changed row, so more indexes mean more work per write, and each index also takes space. The cost is real even though a few writes (for example a row that falls outside a partial index) skip some indexes.

questions.text: A composite index on (last_name, first_name) can efficiently serve which query?

options.text: WHERE first_name = 'Ada'
WHERE last_name = 'Lovelace'
WHERE first_name LIKE '%da'
None of them

questions.explanation: A composite index is ordered by its first column, then the second. A query must use a leftmost prefix of the columns to benefit.

questions.text: Which columns usually deserve an index? Select all that apply.

options.text: A foreign key used in frequent joins
A column in the WHERE clause of a hot query
A boolean column with a 50/50 split, filtered alone on a huge table
Every column, to be safe

questions.explanation: Index what queries actually filter and join on. Low-selectivity columns rarely help on their own, and indexing everything slows writes.

questions.text: EXPLAIN shows a sequential scan on a large table even though an index exists. What is a likely cause?

options.text: The table is too small
The query wraps the indexed column in a function, so the index cannot be used
Indexes only work for integers
The database is offline

questions.explanation: WHERE lower(email) = ... cannot use a plain index on email. Rewrite the predicate or create an index on the expression. Two other usual suspects are a filter that matches a large share of the rows, where a sequential scan really is cheaper, and stale statistics.

questions.text: In PostgreSQL, orders.customer_id is declared as a FOREIGN KEY to customers(id), and you often fetch all orders for one customer. What do you need to do about indexing orders.customer_id?

options.text: Nothing, because PostgreSQL creates an index for every foreign key automatically
Create the index yourself, because PostgreSQL indexes primary keys and unique constraints automatically but not the referencing side of a foreign key
Nothing, because the index on customers(id) already speeds up lookups on orders.customer_id
Nothing, because foreign keys are only indexed when ON DELETE CASCADE is set

questions.explanation: The primary key on customers(id) is indexed, but orders.customer_id is a separate column in a separate table, and PostgreSQL does not index it for you. Without your own index, finding one customer's orders (and checking the foreign key when a customer is deleted) scans the whole orders table.

questions.text: Which single index serves this query best? SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 17 AND created_at >= '2026-01-01' ORDER BY created_at

options.text: (created_at, customer_id)
(customer_id, created_at)
(created_at) alone
(customer_id) alone

questions.explanation: Put the equality column first and the range or sort column second. The index then jumps straight to customer 17 and reads that customer's rows already sorted by created_at from the start date. With (created_at, customer_id) the database has to walk every entry since the start date, for all customers, and check customer_id as it goes. An index on customer_id alone finds the right rows but leaves the date filter and the sort to extra work.

docker-images-containers-and-volumes.title: Docker images, containers, volumes and networks
docker-images-containers-and-volumes.description: Image layers, the writable container layer, what survives a stop or a remove, and how containers reach each other.

questions.text: When Docker creates a container from an image, what does it add on top of the image's read-only layers?

options.text: A full copy of every image layer, so the container can change them freely
One thin writable layer that belongs to that container
A new read-only layer for each process the container starts
A separate virtual disk that replaces the image's filesystem

questions.explanation: Image layers stay read-only and are shared; each container gets only a thin writable layer on top. Copying every layer (option a) is exactly what the layered design avoids, and it would multiply disk use per container.

questions.text: You already have an image built FROM python:3.12-slim and you pull a second image that uses the same base. Why is the second pull fast?

options.text: Docker compresses the second image more aggressively
Docker skips verifying the second image against the registry
The second image is automatically merged into the first one
Layers are content-addressed and shared, so only the layers you do not already have are downloaded

questions.explanation: Identical base layers are stored once and reused, so Docker downloads only the missing ones. The images stay separate; nothing is merged, and nothing is skipped on the verification side.

questions.text: A file written inside a container's filesystem is still there after docker stop followed by docker start on the same container.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: stop and start reuse the same container, including its writable layer. The file is lost only when the container is removed with docker rm and a new one is created.

questions.text: A database container must keep its data after the container is deleted with docker rm and replaced by a fresh docker run. What should you do?

options.text: Let it write to its writable layer and use docker stop instead of docker rm
Add EXPOSE for the data directory in the Dockerfile
Mount a named volume at the database's data directory
Publish the data directory with -p

questions.explanation: A named volume is storage Docker manages outside any container, so it outlives docker rm. The writable layer is deleted with the container, and EXPOSE and -p only deal with network ports, not files.

questions.text: Container svcB runs ping svcA and gets 'bad address'. Both containers were started with docker run and no --network flag. What is the most likely fix?

options.text: Create a user-defined bridge network and start both containers on it, so names resolve through Docker's DNS
Publish svcA with -p so svcB can find it by name
Restart svcB so that it re-reads the hosts file
Switch both containers to the host network and use localhost

questions.explanation: The default bridge network does not resolve container names; a user-defined bridge does. Publishing a port only opens it to the host, so it does nothing for name resolution between containers.

questions.text: Which statements about container networking are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: A server listening on port 8000 in a container answers at localhost:8000 on the host even when -p was not used
localhost inside a container refers to that container's own loopback, not the host
Two containers on a user-defined network should call each other on the host-published port, for example web:8080 after -p 8080:8000
On a shared user-defined network, another container can reach the app as http://web:8000 using its name and container port

questions.explanation: Each container has its own network namespace, so localhost means itself, and peers on a user-defined network use the container name with the container port. The published host port only matters for traffic coming in from outside the container network, and without -p nothing is listening on the host's localhost:8000, so option a is wrong.

questions.text: You ran docker run -d --name broken webapp python -c "print('hi')" and the container shows Exited (0) almost at once, although the image normally starts a Flask server. Why?

options.text: The command after the image name replaced the image's CMD, and that short command finished immediately
The -d flag only works with the image's default command
Python is missing from the image, so the container could not start
The port was not published, so Docker stopped the container

questions.explanation: A container lives only as long as its main process. Overriding CMD with a one-shot command leaves nothing running, and exit code 0 shows it finished normally rather than crashing. Missing Python would give an error and a non-zero exit code.

questions.text: Installing a package inside a running container with docker exec changes the image that the container was started from.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Images are read-only. The change lands in that container's writable layer only, so a container started later from the same image will not have the package; to keep it, add it to the Dockerfile and rebuild.

embeddings-and-vector-search.title: Embeddings and vector search
embeddings-and-vector-search.description: Comparing embeddings with cosine, dot product and L2, why high dimensions behave oddly, chunk sizes, and how pgvector's approximate indexes behave.

questions.text: All the stored vectors and the query are normalised to length 1. Which statement about ranking results is correct?

options.text: Cosine similarity and dot product rank documents differently, because dot product also rewards length
Only cosine similarity gives a stable ranking; L2 distance depends on the query's length
Cosine descending, dot product descending and L2 distance ascending all return the same documents in the same order
L1 (Manhattan) distance is also guaranteed to give the same ranking, because it is a function of the angle

questions.explanation: For unit vectors cosine equals the dot product, and squared L2 distance is 2 - 2*cos, so all three orderings agree. L1 is not a function of the angle and can rank differently even on unit vectors.

questions.text: In pgvector, what does `SELECT id FROM chunks ORDER BY embedding <#> $1 DESC LIMIT 5` return?

options.text: The five most similar chunks, as you would expect from DESC
The five least similar chunks, because <#> is the negative inner product and so already sorts most-similar-first in ascending order
The five chunks closest by cosine distance
An error, because <#> cannot be used in ORDER BY

questions.explanation: Postgres index scans only go ascending, so pgvector negates the inner product. Adding DESC flips it and puts the least similar rows first, and it would also stop an index from being used.

questions.text: A similarity cutoff of 0.8 tuned for cosine similarity can be reused unchanged as a cutoff on L2 distance, because both measure how alike two embeddings are.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The orderings can agree on unit vectors, but the numbers differ. For unit vectors a cosine of 0.8 is an L2 distance of about 0.63, and the direction is reversed (higher cosine is better, lower distance is better). A threshold does not transfer between metrics.

questions.text: What happens to the distances between random points as the number of dimensions grows very large?

options.text: Nearest and farthest neighbours become further apart in relative terms, so search gets easier
Distances shrink toward zero for every pair of points
Distances become exactly equal, so ranking is impossible in principle
The nearest and farthest points end up at almost the same distance, so absolute scores bunch together and fixed thresholds become fragile

questions.explanation: Distance concentration: the relative spread of distances shrinks roughly like 1/sqrt(D). They do not become exactly equal and real embeddings still work because real data has low intrinsic dimension, but you should tune cutoffs on your own labelled queries.

questions.text: A migration creates a table and, in the same step, an IVFFlat index on its empty vector column. The data is loaded afterwards. What is the likely outcome?

options.text: The index works and returns rows without an error, but recall is poor because its clusters were built from no data
Postgres refuses to create the index
The index rebuilds itself automatically as rows arrive
Queries fall back to an exact scan, so results are perfect but slow

questions.explanation: IVFFlat runs k-means over the rows that exist when it is built. On an empty table there is nothing to cluster, so you get only a notice, not an error. Load the data first, then create the index. HNSW has no such training step.

questions.text: Adding an approximate vector index (HNSW or IVFFlat) to a table can change the results of an existing query, unlike a B-tree index.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: A B-tree only changes speed. An approximate index returns the probably-nearest rows, so recall can drop. This is why exact search is used as ground truth when measuring recall.

questions.text: A filtered vector query (WHERE category = 'x' ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 10) on an HNSW index often returns fewer than 10 rows, because the filter runs after the index scan. Which fixes does the lesson describe? Select all that apply.

options.text: Index the filter column, so Postgres can search the matching rows directly
Turn on iterative index scans, so the scan continues until enough rows are found
Lower hnsw.ef_search so the index returns fewer candidates
Put the category condition inside the ORDER BY expression

questions.explanation: The index returns about ef_search candidates and the filter then discards non-matching ones. Indexing the filter column or using iterative scans helps. A lower ef_search makes it worse, and extra expressions in ORDER BY stop the vector index being used at all.

questions.text: An embedding model has a 256-token input limit, but your chunker produces 384-token chunks. What happens?

options.text: The model automatically splits each chunk into two vectors
Every embedding call fails with an error in all cases
Many models silently truncate, so the vector describes only the first 256 tokens while the LLM would still be sent all 384
The vector is built from all 384 tokens, just less precisely

questions.explanation: Sentence-Transformers models truncate text past their max sequence length, so the end of each chunk is invisible to search (some hosted APIs reject over-long input instead). Size chunks in the embedding model's own tokens with a margin.

git-branching-merging-and-rebasing.title: Git branching, merging and rebasing
git-branching-merging-and-rebasing.description: How branches and HEAD work, how merge and rebase differ, and how to undo mistakes safely with revert, reset and the reflog.

questions.text: You are on main and run git switch -c fix, then make one commit. Which statement is true afterwards?

options.text: Both main and fix point to the new commit, because they started at the same place
Only fix moves to the new commit; HEAD follows it and main stays where it was
main moves to the new commit and fix stays put, because main was checked out first
Neither branch moves until the commit has been pushed to a remote

questions.explanation: A branch is just a movable pointer to a commit, and a new commit moves only the branch that HEAD currently follows. After git switch -c fix that branch is fix, so main stays on the older commit, and nothing needs to be pushed for any of this to happen.

questions.text: Nobody has committed to main since you created feature from it, and feature has two new commits. You are on main and run git merge feature. What happens?

options.text: Git fast-forwards main to feature's latest commit and creates no new commit
Git creates a merge commit with two parents, because every merge makes one
Git replays your two commits as brand-new commits on top of main
Git stops with a conflict, because both branches have changed since they split

questions.explanation: Because main is an ancestor of feature, Git has nothing to combine and just slides the main pointer forward. A merge commit with two parents appears only when both branches have new commits, or when you ask for one with --no-ff. Replaying commits as new ones is what rebase does, not merge.

questions.text: Your feature branch is already pushed and a teammate has started working on top of it. You are tempted to run git rebase main on it. What is the main danger?

options.text: It squashes all of your commits into a single one, which hides what each separate change was for
It always produces merge conflicts, even when the changes on the two branches do not overlap
It cannot be undone once it has started, so any mistake destroys your work for good, with no way back
It gives your commits new hashes, so pushing needs a force-push that can erase your teammate's work

questions.explanation: Rebase replays your commits as new ones with new hashes, so history your teammate already has is replaced, and the push needs a force-push that can overwrite what they based their work on. Rebase your own unpublished branches freely and merge shared ones. It can be aborted midway and undone through the reflog, and it keeps your commits and messages.

questions.text: Two branches each edited app.py, one near the top of the file and one near the bottom. What happens when you merge them?

options.text: Git always reports a conflict, because both branches changed the same file
Git keeps the version from the branch you are on and silently drops the other change
Git combines both edits automatically, because they touch different lines
