A thread waiting on network or file I/O releases it, so threads still help I/O-bound programs
Each process started by multiprocessing has its own GIL, so CPU-bound work can use several cores
Adding threads to a CPU-bound pure-Python loop usually makes it run close to N times faster on N cores

questions.explanation: The GIL lets one thread at a time run Python bytecode in a process, but it is released while a thread waits on I/O, and every process has its own, so threads suit I/O-bound work and multiprocessing suits CPU-bound work. It does not make compound operations such as counter += 1 atomic, and it is exactly why extra threads do not speed up CPU-bound pure-Python code.

questions.text: Which statements about dataclasses and __slots__ are true?

options.text: A class that defines __slots__ still accepts any new attribute on its instances, as an ordinary class does
@dataclass generates __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ from the annotated fields
@dataclass makes instances immutable unless you pass frozen=False
A field with a list default must use default_factory=list; a bare [] default raises ValueError
A class with __slots__ normally has no per-instance __dict__, which saves memory per object

questions.explanation: A dataclass generates __init__, __repr__ and __eq__, stays mutable unless you pass frozen=True, and rejects a bare list default so that instances do not share one list. __slots__ replaces the per-instance __dict__ with fixed storage, which saves memory but means attributes that are not listed cannot be added.

questions.text: If you raise a new exception inside an except block without writing from, Python keeps the original exception attached, and the traceback shows both.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Python chains them automatically: the original is stored as __context__ and the traceback prints it first, noting that another exception occurred while handling it. Writing raise NewError from err instead marks err as the direct cause (__cause__), and raise NewError from None is what hides the original.

rag-fundamentals.title: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)
rag-fundamentals.description: When RAG is the right tool, what it does and does not change, and the design choices that decide whether retrieval works.

questions.text: A support assistant must answer questions from internal policy documents that are updated every week, and each answer should point to its source. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Fine-tune the model on the documents every week
Put three example answers in the prompt
RAG: retrieve the relevant passages at query time and put them in the prompt
A multi-agent system with a separate agent per document

questions.explanation: RAG suits facts that are new, private or change often, since nothing is retrained when the documents change, and retrieved passages are inspectable, citable evidence. Fine-tuned behaviour is opaque, with no source to cite.

questions.text: What does RAG change when it answers a question?

options.text: The model's weights, permanently, so it remembers the documents
Which facts are available in the context for this one call, with no change to the model
The tokenizer's vocabulary, adding the documents' terms
The model's default output format and style for all future calls

questions.explanation: Prompting and RAG act at inference time and leave the model untouched. Changing the model's default behaviour, format or style is what fine-tuning is for.

questions.text: Once retrieval supplies the right passages, the model can no longer fabricate, so checking the answer or its citations is unnecessary.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: A model produces fluent text whether or not it is grounded, and nothing guarantees it will say "I don't know" when the context is thin. Production RAG pipelines still ask for sources, tell the model to say when the context does not cover the question, and check the output (for example that citations are real).

questions.text: In a typical RAG request (embed the query, vector search, rerank, call the LLM), which step dominates cost and latency, and what is the most effective optimisation?

options.text: Vector search; use a faster index
Embedding the query; cache every embedding
Reranking; remove the reranker
The LLM call; send fewer tokens by retrieving better rather than retrieving more

questions.explanation: In a typical pipeline the LLM call takes on the order of seconds and costs the most, while embedding, search and rerank take milliseconds to a few hundred (illustrative figures; measure your own). Shaving vector-search time while sending thousands of unnecessary prompt tokens is optimising the wrong thing.

questions.text: Why must long documents be split into chunks before indexing them for RAG? Select all that apply.

options.text: An embedding model reads a limited number of tokens and may silently truncate longer text
One text becomes one vector, so the chunk is the smallest unit retrieval can hand back
The LLM's context is finite and billed per token, and it uses long contexts unevenly
Vector databases cannot store text longer than a page

questions.explanation: These are three separate limits, each enough on its own. Vector databases do not have a page limit; the constraints come from the embedder, the retrieval unit and the LLM's context.

questions.text: A fixed-size chunker cuts the sentence holding the answer into two chunks, so no chunk contains the whole answer. What is the most direct fix?

options.text: Retrieving more chunks per query (a larger k)
Switching to a better embedding model
Changing how documents are chunked, for example overlap or splitting at sentence and heading boundaries
Lowering the LLM's temperature

questions.explanation: The share of answers that sit whole inside some chunk is an upper bound on what a retriever returning single chunks can reach. Better ranking or a better model cannot rebuild a cut answer, and a larger k only helps by luck (both fragments must rank high) while costing tokens, so the dependable fix is at the chunking step.

questions.text: Models use information in the middle of a long context less reliably than at the start or end ("lost in the middle"). Which design choices follow from this? Select all that apply.

options.text: Rerank retrieved chunks and put the most relevant ones where the model uses them best
Avoid adding extra chunks "to be safe", since more context costs more and can lower accuracy
Place the best chunk in the middle, where it is separated from the question
Rely on the model to use every position in the context equally

questions.explanation: Ordering matters, and more context is more expensive, slower and often less accurate. Reranking narrows many candidates to a few good ones and orders them deliberately.

questions.text: Which of these requirements needs tool calling rather than RAG over documents?

options.text: Answering questions about a 400-page employee handbook
Telling a customer whether their order has shipped, using live data from the order system
Rewriting support emails to be more polite
Turning a meeting transcript into action items as JSON

questions.explanation: Live data in an order system is not in any document, so retrieval over documents cannot answer it; the model needs a function to call. The handbook needs RAG, and the email rewrite and transcript summary can be done with a prompt (plus structured output).

redis-data-structures-and-patterns.title: Redis data structures and patterns
redis-data-structures-and-patterns.description: Which Redis type fits which job, plus TTLs and eviction, stampede protection, atomic counters and locks, persistence, scaling out and what blocks the server.

questions.text: Which pair of design choices mostly explains why Redis can answer simple commands in well under a millisecond?

options.text: Values are compressed before they are stored, and every query result is cached again on the client side
Data lives in memory and commands run one at a time on one thread, so there is no disk wait or lock contention
Reads come from disk through a very large page cache, while writes are only flushed to the storage device once an hour
Commands run in parallel on every CPU core, and fine-grained row locks keep them from interfering

questions.explanation: Redis holds the whole dataset in RAM, so a command never waits for a disk read, and one thread executes commands one at a time, so there are no locks to fight over and no cost for switching between threads. Disk is used only for persistence, and neither compression nor extra CPU cores is what makes it quick.

questions.text: Which statements about choosing a Redis data type are correct?

options.text: A hash suits an object such as a user profile, where you read or change one field without rewriting the rest
A sorted set suits a leaderboard, because its members stay ordered by score and the top few can be read directly
A set suits a timeline, because it keeps its members in the order they were added and lets you page through them
A list suits looking up one item by its value in constant time, because lists are indexed by value, not by position

questions.explanation: A hash groups related fields under one key, and a sorted set keeps unique members ranked by a numeric score. A set is unordered and holds each member once, so it fits membership tests and intersections rather than timelines. A list is ordered by position, so finding an item by its value means scanning it.

questions.text: In a cache-aside setup, a very popular key expires and 2,000 requests miss at the same moment, each rebuilding the same expensive value from the database. What is the standard way to stop this?

options.text: Add more database replicas so that each of the 2,000 identical queries runs a little faster than before
Have every client retry immediately, in a tight loop, until the value finally shows up in the cache again
Switch the cache to write-through, so that the key is always rewritten well before it has a chance to expire
Let one request take a short SET NX EX lock and rebuild the value while the rest wait or use a stale copy

questions.explanation: When many requests miss together they all repeat the same expensive rebuild and can overwhelm the database. The fix is to let one winner hold a short lock (SET key value NX EX seconds), rebuild the value and refill the cache while the others wait briefly or serve a slightly stale copy. Extra replicas only make duplicate work cheaper, tight retries make the pile-up worse, and write-through does not stop keys from expiring or being evicted.

questions.text: Overwriting a key that has a TTL with a plain SET (no expiry option) keeps the old TTL, so the key still expires on schedule.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: SET replaces the value and discards any existing TTL unless you pass EX or PX again, or use KEEPTTL. A cache refresh that forgets this quietly turns an expiring key into one that lives until it is evicted or deleted.

questions.text: One Redis instance holds both disposable cache entries and login sessions, with maxmemory-policy set to allkeys-lru. When memory runs short, some users are suddenly logged out. Why?

options.text: allkeys-lru may evict any key, sessions included, so data you cannot lose needs an instance that does not evict
LRU removes the oldest keys by creation time, and the sessions happen to be the oldest keys in the instance
Keys that carry a TTL, as sessions usually do, are evicted first under every LRU policy, whatever else is stored
Redis evicts the largest keys first when memory is short, and session objects are bigger than cache entries

questions.explanation: allkeys-lru treats every key as a candidate, so a cache that shares an instance with sessions can lose sessions along with cache entries. Keep must-not-lose data on a separate instance that does not evict, or use volatile-lru and give only the cache entries a TTL. LRU means least recently used, not oldest, largest or soonest to expire.

questions.text: A worker takes a lock with SET lock:report abc123 NX EX 30, does its job, then releases it with DEL lock:report. What is the main weakness of this pattern?

options.text: NX makes the SET block until the lock is free, so a worker that asks for the lock can end up waiting forever
SET with NX and EX is really two separate commands, so two workers can both believe that they now hold the lock
If the job overruns 30 seconds, another worker gets the lock, and the first worker's DEL then deletes theirs
EX makes Redis delete the key from every replica at once, so the lock can vanish long before the job is finished

questions.explanation: The lock can expire while the first worker is still running; a second worker then acquires it, and the first worker's unconditional DEL removes the second worker's lock. Store a unique token as the value, release only if it still matches (a short Lua script makes the check and the delete one atomic step), and size the TTL to the job. SET with NX and EX is one atomic command, and NX returns at once rather than waiting.

questions.text: A fixed-window rate limiter that runs INCR on a per-minute counter key can let a client send almost twice the limit in a short burst that straddles two windows.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: A client can use its whole allowance in the last second of one minute and again in the first second of the next, and each window still looks within its limit. A sliding window (for example a sorted set of request timestamps) or a token bucket smooths this out, at the cost of more work per request.

questions.text: A Redis server holds data you would hate to lose. It takes an RDB snapshot every 15 minutes and has AOF switched off. What can you lose if it crashes, and what is the usual way to lose less?

options.text: Nothing, because Redis writes a final snapshot as it goes down; AOF would only help with disk space
Only the few commands in flight at that instant; AOF is needed for replicas and not for crash recovery
Everything, because an RDB file cannot be loaded after a crash, and only an AOF can be replayed at start-up
Up to the last 15 minutes of writes; AOF with fsync every second would cut that to about a second

questions.explanation: An RDB file is a point-in-time snapshot, so everything written after the latest one is gone after a crash. AOF logs every write, and with fsync once per second it limits the loss to about a second (fsync on every write loses the least but is the slowest). A crashed process does not get to write a final snapshot, and RDB files do load fine at start-up.

questions.text: Redis executes commands one at a time on a single main thread. Which of these can make every other client wait?

options.text: Running KEYS * on a database that holds millions of keys
Reading a hash with millions of fields in a single HGETALL call
Running INCR on a counter key that a thousand clients update every second
Setting a short string value with SET and an expiry time on a busy instance
Running a Lua script that loops over millions of elements

questions.explanation: Anything that touches every element, such as KEYS, HGETALL on a huge hash or a long-running script, holds the single thread until it finishes, so every other client queues behind it. INCR and SET on a small value take microseconds. Use SCAN and HSCAN to walk the data in small batches, and avoid giant keys.

questions.text: A Redis primary is using 90% of its machine's RAM and the dataset keeps growing. Which change actually addresses that?

options.text: Add read replicas, so that the data is spread across more machines
Shard the keys across several primaries, for example with Redis Cluster
Turn on AOF, so that older data can be kept on disk instead of in memory
Set maxmemory above the machine's RAM, so that the operating system swaps the rest

questions.explanation: A replica is a full copy of its primary, so it needs just as much memory and does nothing for capacity. Redis Cluster splits the keys across primaries by hash slot, so each node holds only a share. AOF is a durability log, not a way to hold data outside memory, and swapping makes Redis latency collapse.

replication-and-sharding.title: Replication and sharding
replication-and-sharding.description: What read replicas fix, what replication lag breaks, how shard keys work, and what sharding costs you.

questions.text: A single primary database is saturated by write traffic. Which change addresses that?

options.text: Add more read replicas
Shard the data horizontally across several primaries
Switch replication from asynchronous to synchronous
Promote a replica and keep the old primary as a standby

questions.explanation: Every write still goes through the one primary, so replicas do not help write throughput. Sharding spreads rows, and so writes, across many primaries.

questions.text: A user posts a comment, is redirected to the page, and their comment is missing. Refreshing a second later shows it. What is the likely cause and the standard fix?

options.text: The write failed; retry it with a longer timeout
The primary rolled back; add a unique index
The read hit a replica that was behind (replication lag); route reads that must see the user's own write to the primary
The cache is full; raise its memory limit

questions.explanation: This is a read-your-own-writes violation: the write was committed on the primary but the replica had not applied it yet. Sending that particular read to the primary, or waiting for the replica to catch up, fixes it.

questions.text: With asynchronous replication, a write the client was told succeeded can be lost if the primary crashes and a lagging replica is promoted.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Async replication acknowledges the client without waiting for any replica, so the newly promoted primary may never have received the last transactions. Synchronous replication closes that gap at the price of write latency.

questions.text: What is the main cost of synchronous replication to a required standby?

options.text: Reads become eventually consistent
Every write waits for the standby, and writes can block if that standby is unreachable
The primary can no longer take writes from more than one client
Replicas stop being able to serve reads

questions.explanation: Waiting for a replica confirmation adds a network round trip to every commit, and with the required replica down the primary cannot acknowledge writes. It trades availability and latency for durability.

questions.text: Rows are placed with hash(customer_id) % N. What is the main advantage, and a main drawback?

options.text: Range queries stay on one shard; but hot spots are common
Load spreads evenly; but range queries scatter across shards and changing N moves most rows unless you use consistent hashing
Cross-shard joins become cheap; but ids are no longer unique
Rebalancing is trivial; but the shard map is a single point of failure

questions.explanation: Hashing gives an even spread and avoids hot spots, which range-based sharding does not. The costs are scattered range queries and reshuffling when N changes. Option d describes directory-based sharding.

questions.text: Which of these get harder or stop working when a database is sharded across machines? Select all that apply.

options.text: Joins between rows that live on different shards
An ACID transaction that updates rows on two shards
Looking up a row when the query includes the shard key
Globally unique ids from a per-database auto-increment sequence

questions.explanation: Joins, transactions and sequences are all per-database features, so they break across shard boundaries. A query that carries the shard key is routed to one shard and works as before.

questions.text: Declarative table partitioning inside a single PostgreSQL server is sharding, and it scales write capacity beyond one machine.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Partitioning splits one logical table into pieces on the same machine, which helps manageability and some query speed. Sharding spreads data over independent databases, which is what raises the write and capacity ceiling.

questions.text: You shard an events table by date range, one shard per month. What problem should you expect?

options.text: Every current write lands on the newest shard, creating a hot spot
Range queries over a month must scan every shard
Adding a new month forces most existing rows to move
Ids can no longer be generated at all

questions.explanation: With time-based ranges, all new writes target the current period's shard while older shards sit idle. Range queries within one month actually stay on one shard, which is the strength of range-based sharding.

secrets-hashing-and-encryption-basics.title: Secrets, hashing and encryption basics
secrets-hashing-and-encryption-basics.description: The difference between encoding, hashing and encryption, how passwords should be stored, and how to keep keys and secrets out of the wrong places.

questions.text: Which statements about encoding, hashing and encryption are correct?

options.text: Base64 is an encoding, so anyone can turn it back into the original data without a key
A hash is one-way: you can compute it from the data, but you cannot recover the data from it
Encryption is one-way, so encrypted data can never be read again
Hashing and encryption are the same thing, because both scramble data

questions.explanation: Encoding such as Base64 only changes the format, so it hides nothing, and a hash is a one-way fingerprint that has no key. Encryption is the reversible one: with the right key you get the original back. Mixing them up leads to mistakes like 'protecting' a secret with Base64 or hoping to decrypt a hash.

questions.text: Why should a login system store a hash of each password rather than an encrypted copy of it?

options.text: Hashes are smaller, so they take up much less room in the users table of the database
Encrypted passwords cannot be compared with whatever the user types in at login time
Encryption is far slower than hashing, so each login would take much too long to finish
A hash is one-way, so a stolen database cannot simply be decrypted back into passwords

questions.explanation: To log someone in you only need to check a guess, which you can do by hashing the guess and comparing hashes. With encryption, anyone who steals the database together with the key, which the server must keep somewhere, gets every password back. Size and speed are not the reason.

questions.text: What does adding a unique random salt to each password before hashing achieve?

options.text: It makes each hash faster to compute, which cuts the login time on the server
Equal passwords end up with different hashes, and precomputed tables become useless
It acts as a secret key kept outside the database, so a stolen database cannot be cracked
It encrypts the hash so that only the application server is able to read it

questions.explanation: A salt is a random value stored next to the hash; it is not secret. It makes every hash unique, so an attacker cannot reuse one table of precomputed hashes against all users or spot who shares a password. A secret kept outside the database is called a pepper, which is a different tool.

questions.text: Why is a single round of SHA-256 a poor way to store passwords, when bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2 are recommended?

options.text: SHA-256 has been broken, so attackers can simply reverse every hash back into a password
SHA-256 cannot be used with a salt, so equal passwords always give the same hash
SHA-256 is designed to be fast, so attackers can test billions of guesses per second
SHA-256 output is too short to tell different passwords apart with any real reliability

questions.explanation: Password hashes are deliberately slow (and, for scrypt and Argon2, memory-hungry), with a cost setting you can raise as hardware improves, so a thief with a leaked database must pay heavily for every guess. SHA-256 is not broken and can be salted; it is just far too cheap to compute for this job.

questions.text: How does a TLS (HTTPS) connection use asymmetric and symmetric cryptography?

options.text: Public-key methods verify the server and agree a key; symmetric encryption protects the data
Symmetric keys prove the server's identity, and asymmetric keys then encrypt all of the traffic
Asymmetric encryption protects every byte of the traffic, because it is the stronger kind
Only symmetric keys are used, and the certificate is a password that the user types in

questions.explanation: Asymmetric (public and private key) operations are comparatively slow, but they let two strangers prove identity through the certificate and agree on a secret over an open network. Symmetric encryption with that shared key, such as AES, is fast, so it carries the bulk of the traffic. Nobody types a password for this.

questions.text: A service sends webhooks with a plain SHA-256 hash of the body in a header, so receivers can detect tampering. Why is that not enough?

options.text: SHA-256 is too weak for tamper detection, so a longer hash such as SHA-512 is needed
Whoever changes the body can compute a new hash; an HMAC needs a shared secret key
HTTP headers are not allowed to carry hash values, so the hash must go in the body
It is enough, because a one-way hash cannot be forged by someone who changes the body

questions.explanation: A plain hash has no key, so an attacker who edits the body simply recomputes the hash and swaps it in; being one-way does not make it unforgeable. An HMAC mixes in a secret shared by sender and receiver, so only a key holder can produce a valid tag. A longer hash without a key has the same flaw.

questions.text: A team can safely design its own encryption scheme, as long as it keeps the algorithm secret.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Security should rest on the secrecy of the key, never on hiding how the scheme works, and home-made schemes almost always hide subtle flaws that only experts find. Use well-reviewed algorithms such as AES-GCM through a trusted library, and let the library handle details like nonces.

questions.text: Which of these are sensible ways to give a deployed service its database password?

options.text: Store it in a secret manager and let the service fetch it when it starts
Put it in a config file in the repository, because the repository is private
Set it as an environment variable in the deployment, outside the code and the image
Copy a .env file that contains it into the container image

questions.explanation: Both good options keep the value out of the code and out of the image: a secret manager adds access control, audit logs and easy rotation, and an environment variable set at deploy time is a simpler step up, though it can show up in process listings and crash reports. Anything copied into an image or committed to a repository lives on in image layers and git history, available to anyone who can pull them.

questions.text: A developer commits an API key to a repository and deletes it in the next commit. What should the team do?

options.text: Nothing is needed, because the latest version of the file no longer contains the key
Make the repository private, because the key then stays safe from now on
Treat the key as leaked: revoke it, issue a new one and store that one safely
Rewrite the git history with a force-push, then carry on using the same old key

questions.explanation: Git keeps every earlier commit, and clones, forks, caches and bots that scan public repositories may already hold the key, so deleting it from the latest commit protects nothing. The safe response is to revoke and replace (rotate) it, then clean the history and check the logs for misuse. Planned rotation works the same way, with the old and new key valid side by side for a while so nothing breaks.

questions.text: A password-reset token generated with Math.random() or a timestamp is safe as long as the token is long enough.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Ordinary random functions and timestamps are predictable: an attacker who sees some outputs can often work out the next ones, so extra length does not help. Use a cryptographically secure generator, such as crypto.randomBytes in Node, secrets.token_urlsafe in Python or the operating system's random source.

sessions-and-cookies.title: Sessions and cookies
sessions-and-cookies.description: How a server remembers who you are between requests, and the cookie settings that keep that safe.

questions.text: Which cookie attribute stops JavaScript on the page from reading the cookie?

options.text: Secure
HttpOnly
SameSite
Path

questions.explanation: HttpOnly hides the cookie from document.cookie, so a cross-site scripting bug cannot simply read the session id.

questions.text: Which attributes should a session cookie normally set? Select all that apply.

options.text: HttpOnly
Secure
SameSite
An expiry far in the future so users never log in again

questions.explanation: HttpOnly limits script access, Secure keeps the cookie off plain HTTP, SameSite limits cross-site sending. A session that never expires is a risk, not a feature.

questions.text: Issuing a new session id when a user logs in helps prevent session fixation.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: If an attacker planted a known session id before login, replacing it at login makes that id worthless.

questions.text: In a server-side session design, where is the user's state kept?

options.text: In the cookie itself
On the server, found by the session id in the cookie
In the URL
In the browser's localStorage

questions.explanation: The cookie holds only an opaque id. The state lives in memory, Redis or a database on the server, which is also why a session can be revoked instantly.

questions.text: Why must a session id be long and random?

options.text: So the cookie is easy to read
So it cannot be guessed or enumerated by an attacker
To make the cookie smaller
So it sorts well in the database

questions.explanation: Anyone who guesses a valid id becomes that user. Use a cryptographically secure random generator and enough bits that guessing is hopeless.

sql-joins-and-grouping.title: SQL joins, grouping and NULL
sql-joins-and-grouping.description: Which join to pick, how WHERE and HAVING differ, and the NULL and join-grain traps that quietly return wrong numbers.

questions.text: You need a report of every customer and how many orders each has, including customers with zero orders. Which join fits?

options.text: INNER JOIN from customers to orders
CROSS JOIN from customers to orders
LEFT JOIN from customers to orders
INNER JOIN from orders to customers

questions.explanation: A LEFT JOIN keeps every customer and fills the order columns with NULL when nothing matches. An INNER JOIN, in either direction, drops customers with no orders, so the report silently understates the customer list.

questions.text: Why does SELECT c.name, count(*) AS n FROM ... WHERE n > 2 fail, while ORDER BY n works?

options.text: ORDER BY is the only clause allowed to use aliases, by the SQL standard's syntax rules
WHERE runs before SELECT, so the alias does not exist yet; ORDER BY runs after SELECT
n is a reserved word, which only works in ORDER BY
WHERE runs after GROUP BY, and grouped rows cannot be filtered

questions.explanation: The logical order is FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT. An alias is created at the SELECT step, and the aggregate does not exist until grouping. Option d has it backwards: WHERE runs before GROUP BY.

questions.text: You want customers who have placed at least 3 orders. Where does the condition go?

options.text: In HAVING count(o.id) >= 3, after GROUP BY
In WHERE count(o.id) >= 3
In the ON clause of the join
In ORDER BY count(o.id) >= 3

questions.explanation: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping and cannot use aggregates. HAVING filters whole groups after aggregation, which is exactly what a count threshold needs.

questions.text: A teammate writes: SELECT c.name, o.total_cents FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.total_cents > 1000. Customers with no orders vanish. Why?

options.text: LEFT JOIN only keeps customers who have at least one order over the limit
The database rewrites every LEFT JOIN into a RIGHT JOIN when WHERE is present
total_cents must be indexed for a LEFT JOIN to keep unmatched rows
Unmatched rows have NULL in total_cents, and WHERE total_cents > 1000 rejects NULL, turning the join back into an inner join

questions.explanation: WHERE runs after the join and a comparison with NULL is never true, so the preserved no-match rows are filtered out. Put the condition on the optional table in the ON clause instead (ON ... AND o.total_cents > 1000).

questions.text: After customers LEFT JOIN orders, grouped by customer, which expressions give 0 for a customer with no orders? Select all that apply.

options.text: count(o.id)
count(*)
COALESCE(sum(o.total_cents), 0)
sum(o.total_cents)

questions.explanation: count(column) skips NULLs, so the placeholder row counts as zero, and COALESCE turns the NULL sum into 0. count(*) counts the placeholder row and returns 1, and a bare sum() over only NULLs returns NULL.

questions.text: WHERE deleted_at = NULL returns the rows where deleted_at is not set.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: NULL means unknown, so NULL = NULL is itself NULL, not true, and the query matches nothing. Use deleted_at IS NULL.

questions.text: A query on tables of 1,000 and 2,000 rows returns about 2,000,000 rows and hangs. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: A missing index on the primary key
A missing or wrong join condition, which produced a cross join
Using INNER JOIN instead of EXISTS
Using ORDER BY without LIMIT

questions.explanation: Without a join condition every left row pairs with every right row, so the row count is left times right. A missing index makes a query slow but does not change how many rows come back.

questions.text: After joining customers to orders, summing a per-customer column such as credit_limit counts each customer's value once per order.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The join changes the grain of the result to one row per order, so a customer with three orders appears three times and their credit limit is triple-counted. Summing an order-level value such as total_cents is fine.

sql-window-functions-and-query-tuning.title: SQL window functions and query tuning
sql-window-functions-and-query-tuning.description: Ranking, running totals and LAG with window functions, then reading EXPLAIN plans and fixing slow queries: SARGability, N+1 and pagination.

questions.text: Scores sorted from highest to lowest are 100, 90, 90 and 80. For the row with 80, what do RANK() and DENSE_RANK() return?

options.text: RANK 3 and DENSE_RANK 3
RANK 4 and DENSE_RANK 3
RANK 4 and DENSE_RANK 4
RANK 3 and DENSE_RANK 4

questions.explanation: RANK leaves a gap after a tie, giving 1, 2, 2, 4, while DENSE_RANK does not, giving 1, 2, 2, 3. ROW_NUMBER would number the rows 1, 2, 3, 4 and pick an arbitrary order between the tied rows.

questions.text: A query selects ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC) AS rn and adds WHERE rn = 1 to keep each customer's latest order. It fails. Why, and what is the fix?

options.text: WHERE runs before window functions, so rn does not exist yet; filter in an outer query or a CTE
ROW_NUMBER cannot be combined with PARTITION BY unless the query also contains a GROUP BY clause
Window functions are allowed only in the ORDER BY clause, so the whole expression has to move there
rn is a reserved word in SQL, so the alias has to be written in quotes before it can be used

questions.explanation: The logical order is FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, then the SELECT list where window functions are computed, so neither a window result nor its alias is available to WHERE. Put the window query in a CTE or subquery and filter on rn in the outer query.

questions.text: SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY sale_day) is used for a running total, and two rows share the same sale_day. What do those two rows show by default?

options.text: Different totals, because the database adds the rows one at a time in the order they happen to be stored
NULL for both, because a tie makes the running order ambiguous and the sum cannot be defined
An error, because the ORDER BY inside OVER must be unique for the frame to be computed
The same total for both, including both amounts, because tied rows count as peers in the default frame

questions.explanation: With an ORDER BY and no explicit frame, the default is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, which includes every row that ties with the current one on the sort key. For strict row-by-row totals write ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, or add a unique tiebreaker column to the ORDER BY.

questions.text: orders has an index on created_at, but WHERE DATE(created_at) = '2025-03-01' still scans the whole table. What is the problem, and the usual fix?

options.text: The index only supports equality on exact timestamps, so the column has to be cast to text first
DATE() is deprecated, so the planner skips every index when a query uses it in a condition
A function on the column hides it from the index; compare the bare column with a range
Timestamp columns cannot be indexed at all; add a separate date column and index that one instead

questions.explanation: The planner can use a plain B-tree index only when the indexed column appears on its own, so wrapping it in DATE() forces a scan that evaluates the function on every row. Rewrite the condition as created_at >= '2025-03-01' AND created_at < '2025-03-02', or create an index on the expression itself.

questions.text: A feed endpoint runs ORDER BY id LIMIT 20 OFFSET 200000 and gets slower the deeper the page. Which change addresses the cause?

options.text: Add a second index on id, so the database can skip the first 200000 rows without reading them
Raise the LIMIT to 200, so there are fewer pages and the offsets stay smaller overall
Run SELECT COUNT(*) first, so the planner knows the table size and can plan the skip
Pass the last id seen and query WHERE id > :last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT 20

questions.explanation: With OFFSET the database still has to walk past and discard all 200000 earlier rows before it returns 20, so the cost grows with the page number. Keyset (seek) pagination uses the index to jump straight to the first row after the last id seen, so each page costs about the same and rows added meanwhile do not shift the pages.

questions.text: A page shows 50 orders, and for each order the code runs SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id = ?, so 51 queries run in all. What is the problem, and the usual fix?

options.text: customers.id needs an index; once it has one, the 51 queries are fast enough and nothing else changes
It is an N+1 pattern; load the customers with a JOIN or one WHERE id IN (...) query
Nothing needs fixing, because the database caches the 50 lookups and runs them as one
The queries should be wrapped in one transaction, which turns them into a single round trip

questions.explanation: One query for the list plus one per row is the N+1 pattern: the cost is 51 round trips and 51 plans, not slow individual lookups. A JOIN or a single WHERE id IN (...) query needs one or two queries whatever N is. A transaction does not merge queries into one round trip, and an index would only speed up each of the 50 lookups a little.

questions.text: Which statements about reading query plans with EXPLAIN are true?

options.text: A plain EXPLAIN, without ANALYZE, runs the query and reports its real timings
A Seq Scan can be the cheapest plan when the query needs a large share of the table's rows
An Index Scan is always faster than a Seq Scan, so every Seq Scan node is a bug
A big gap between estimated and actual rows in EXPLAIN ANALYZE often points to stale or too-coarse statistics
EXPLAIN ANALYZE on an UPDATE really performs the update, so wrap it in a transaction you roll back

questions.explanation: A Seq Scan is the cheapest plan when most of the table is needed, so it is not automatically a problem, and a plain EXPLAIN only shows the plan without running anything. ANALYZE executes the statement and adds actual rows and timings, so a row estimate far from the real count suggests stale statistics, and an UPDATE or DELETE under ANALYZE changes data unless you roll back.

questions.text: Which statements about WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING are true?

options.text: HAVING filters groups after aggregation, so it can test results such as COUNT(*) > 5
WHERE COUNT(*) > 5 is valid and keeps only the groups with more than five rows
Rows removed by WHERE never reach the aggregate functions, so they are not counted or summed
A plain-column condition such as status = 'paid' runs faster in HAVING than in WHERE, because HAVING sees fewer rows
COUNT(column) skips rows where the column is NULL, while COUNT(*) counts every row

questions.explanation: WHERE decides which rows get grouped, so removed rows never reach COUNT or SUM, while HAVING filters the finished groups and is where an aggregate condition belongs. An aggregate in WHERE is an error, and a plain-column condition belongs in WHERE rather than HAVING because it can then discard rows before the grouping work is done. COUNT(*) counts rows, but COUNT(column) ignores NULLs.

questions.text: In PostgreSQL 12 and later, a simple non-recursive CTE that is referenced only once is normally inlined into the outer query, so the planner can push filters and use indexes through it.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Before version 12 every CTE was computed on its own and acted as an optimisation fence. Now a side-effect-free CTE used once is folded in like a subquery; writing AS MATERIALIZED restores the old behaviour, and a CTE referenced more than once is materialized by default.

questions.text: Comparing each row with the previous row's value, such as a day-over-day revenue change, requires a self-join, because window functions cannot read other rows.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day) returns the previous row's value, and LEAD returns the next row's, so the comparison needs no self-join. At the edge of a partition they return NULL unless you pass a default, and PARTITION BY restarts the lookback for each group.

system-design-availability-latency-and-s.title: Availability, latency, throughput and single points of failure
system-design-availability-latency-and-s.description: The nines, availability in series and in parallel, Little's Law, percentile latency and finding single points of failure.

questions.text: A service promises 99.9% availability over a year. About how much downtime does that allow?

options.text: About 53 minutes
About 3.7 days
About 36 hours
About 8.8 hours

questions.explanation: 0.1% of 8,760 hours in a year is about 8.8 hours. About 53 minutes is 99.99% (four nines), and about 3.7 days is 99%.

questions.text: A request must pass through a web tier and then a database, in series. Each is 99.9% available and they fail independently. What is the availability of the pair?

options.text: About 99.8%
About 99.95%

questions.explanation: In series you multiply: 0.999 x 0.999 = 0.998, so each extra required component lowers the total. The pair can never be better than its weakest part. 99.99% would be the result for two redundant copies, not a chain.

questions.text: Two identical servers each have 99% availability, fail independently, and either one can serve all traffic. What is the availability of the pair?
questions.explanation: The service is down only when both are down: 0.01 x 0.01 = 0.0001, so availability is 99.99%. This assumes independent failures and working failover, which is why two instances in one rack or behind one shared dependency do not get this benefit.

questions.text: By Little's Law, how many requests are in flight on average when a service handles 5,000 requests per second and each takes 50 ms?
questions.explanation: Concurrency = throughput x latency = 5,000 per second x 0.05 s = 250. The tempting 100,000 comes from dividing by 0.05 instead of multiplying, and 25 comes from treating 50 ms as 0.005 s.

questions.text: Which of these are single points of failure? Select all that apply.

options.text: One Redis instance that holds the sessions for every app server
Four stateless app servers spread across two availability zones
One database primary with no standby or replica
Two load balancers sharing a virtual IP, with automatic failover

questions.explanation: If the only Redis or the only database primary dies, everything that depends on it stops, however many app servers sit in front. Redundant stateless servers and a failover pair of load balancers are the fixes, not the problem.

questions.text: A dashboard shows an average latency of 80 ms and a p99 of 300 ms. What does the p99 figure mean?

options.text: 99% of requests finished in 300 ms or less, and the slowest 1% took longer
The average of the slowest 1% of requests is 300 ms
300 ms is the longest any request has taken
Requests are 99% likely to take exactly 300 ms

questions.explanation: A percentile is a cut-off: p99 is the value that 99% of requests stay under. The tail can be far worse than the cut-off, and the average hides it, which is why latency targets are written as percentiles.

questions.text: Shortening the time it takes to recover from a failure can raise availability as much as making failures less frequent.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Availability is roughly MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR), so cutting the repair time raises it just as lengthening the time between failures does. Automated failover that turns a 30-minute outage into 30 seconds is often easier than preventing the failure.

questions.text: If one server handles 1,000 requests per second, 10 servers will always handle 10,000 requests per second.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Scaling is linear only when nothing is shared. A shared database, lock or other serial part caps the gain (Amdahl's Law), so the added servers deliver less than 10x.

tcp-ip-dns-ports-and-nat.title: TCP, DNS, ports and NAT
tcp-ip-dns-ports-and-nat.description: How a name becomes an address, how a connection reaches the right program, and what the failure messages tell you.

questions.text: A client tries to connect to a server's port and gets "Connection refused" almost instantly. What is the most likely situation?

options.text: A firewall is silently dropping the SYN packets
The server's host is powered off
The host is reachable, but nothing is listening on that port
The domain name failed to resolve

questions.explanation: A host with no listening socket on the port answers with a TCP reset, which the client reports at once as refused. A silent drop or a dead host gives no reply, so the client waits and times out; a DNS failure would never get as far as a connection.

questions.text: Seeing many sockets in TIME-WAIT on a busy client is a sign that the application is leaking connections.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: TIME-WAIT is how TCP lets a recently closed connection linger briefly to catch stray packets, and it clears on its own. A growing pile of CLOSE-WAIT is the one that usually points to an application that forgets to close sockets.

questions.text: A service answers curl http://127.0.0.1:8080 on its own machine, but other hosts cannot connect. Which explanation and check fit best?

options.text: It is bound to 127.0.0.1 only; ss -tlnp shows 127.0.0.1:8080 instead of 0.0.0.0:8080
TCP does not allow more than one client per port; ss -tan shows the active client
Port 8080 is a privileged port; ls -l shows who owns the binary
The DNS TTL is too long; dig +trace shows the delay

questions.explanation: A socket bound to the loopback address is invisible to every other host, and ss -tlnp shows the address it is bound to. One listening port serves many clients, 8080 is not below 1024, and DNS is not involved when the address is already known.

questions.text: dig example.com returns the correct IP, but curl example.com connects to a different machine. What should you check first?

options.text: Whether the TCP three-way handshake is being retransmitted
Whether the server certificate has expired
Whether the DNS record is a CNAME or an A record
Whether /etc/hosts has an entry for that name

questions.explanation: Applications resolve names through the system resolver, which normally reads /etc/hosts before asking DNS, while dig always queries a DNS server. When dig and getent or curl disagree, a hosts-file override is the first suspect.

questions.text: Which statements about DNS are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: A CNAME record maps a name to another name, which the resolver then looks up
An A record maps a name to an IPv6 address
Lowering a record's TTL before a planned change makes the change take effect sooner
A DNS TTL is a hop counter that routers decrement

questions.explanation: CNAME is an alias, and a short TTL means caches refetch sooner, so operators lower it ahead of a migration. IPv6 addresses live in AAAA records, and the hop counter is the unrelated TTL field in the IP header; a DNS TTL is a caching lifetime in seconds.

questions.text: A host is configured as 10.0.5.40/29. Which of these addresses is on the same local network?
questions.explanation: A /29 has 8 addresses, so blocks start at multiples of 8 and this one spans 10.0.5.40 to 10.0.5.47. 10.0.5.39 and 10.0.5.48 sit in the neighbouring blocks, and 10.0.6.41 is a different third octet entirely, so the host would send those to its gateway.

questions.text: A container on a private address behind NAT can usually open connections to the internet, but an outside host cannot start a connection to it unless a port forward is configured.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: NAT creates its translation entry when the inside host sends the first packet out, so replies can find their way back. With no entry and a non-routable private address, unsolicited inbound traffic has nowhere to go until a port forward (destination NAT) maps it.

questions.text: Which workloads fit UDP better than TCP? Select all that apply.

options.text: Transferring a file where every byte must arrive intact
A DNS query and its short response
A database client talking to its server
A live voice call where a late packet is useless

questions.explanation: UDP skips the handshake and retransmission, which suits small request/response exchanges and real-time media where timeliness beats completeness. Files and database traffic need TCP's reliable, ordered delivery.

testing-strategies-for-backends.title: Testing strategies for backends
testing-strategies-for-backends.description: The test pyramid, test doubles, real versus in-memory databases, flaky tests, contract tests, and what code coverage can and cannot tell you.

questions.text: A team's suite has 5 unit tests, 20 integration tests and 400 browser-driven end-to-end tests. It takes 90 minutes and a few tests fail at random on every run. What does the test pyramid suggest?

options.text: Add even more end-to-end tests, because only they show what real users will actually see and experience when they use it
Move checks down: many unit tests for the logic, fewer integration tests for the seams, a few end-to-end tests
Delete the integration tests, since the end-to-end tests already exercise everything they would check
Run the 400 end-to-end tests in parallel on bigger machines and accept the occasional random failure

questions.explanation: Unit tests (one piece in isolation) are fast and point straight at the failure, integration tests (several pieces with real dependencies such as a database) catch problems at the seams, and end-to-end tests (the whole system, as a user would use it) are slow, flaky and costly, so you keep few of them. A suite shaped like an upside-down pyramid is slow and flaky because the slowest tests carry most of the load, and more of them or bigger machines does not fix that.

questions.text: Which statements about test doubles are correct?

options.text: A stub returns canned answers so the code under test can run, for example a payment client that always says 'approved'
A mock also verifies how it was used, for example that charge() was called once with the right amount
A fake is a simplified but working implementation, for example an in-memory repository backed by a dictionary
A stub makes the test fail if the code under test never calls it
A fake is the real production dependency, started for the duration of the test

questions.explanation: A stub supplies inputs, a mock verifies interactions and a fake offers a working shortcut; all three replace real collaborators so the code under test can run in isolation. Failing when a call never happens is mock behaviour, not stub behaviour, and a fake is a stand-in rather than the real system.

questions.text: A test asserts that OrderService calls repo.save() exactly once with particular arguments. After a harmless refactor that batches several saves into one call, the test fails although the behaviour is unchanged. What does this show?

options.text: The refactor was a mistake, because a correct refactor can never make an existing test fail
The test needs more verifications, such as the order of every call, to catch problems sooner
Mocks should never be used for writes, because a mock cannot reliably record a call to save()
The test is tied to how the code works, not what it does; checking results would survive it

questions.explanation: Verifying exact calls ties a test to the implementation, so it fails on harmless refactors and its false alarms teach people to ignore red builds. Prefer asserting on observable results (the saved orders, the response) and use a fake collaborator, keeping interaction checks for effects that are the point, such as 'an email was sent'.

questions.text: Integration tests for a PostgreSQL-backed service could use an in-memory substitute such as SQLite, or a throwaway PostgreSQL container. Which are good reasons to prefer the real engine?

options.text: A query that relies on a PostgreSQL feature can pass or fail differently on the substitute than in production
Constraints, transaction isolation and locking behave as they do in production, so integrity and concurrency bugs show up
The real engine always starts faster than an in-memory database
With a real engine, unit tests are no longer needed
Migrations run on the engine production uses, so a broken migration fails the build instead of the release

questions.explanation: The database is exactly the seam an integration test exists to check, and engines differ in SQL dialect, types, constraints, locking and migration behaviour, so a substitute can hide real failures. A container is usually slower to start than an in-memory database, and integration tests complement unit tests rather than replacing them.

questions.text: A test creates an order and asserts that its created_at equals the current time. It passes most runs but fails now and then. What is the most robust fix?

options.text: Loosen the assertion to accept any time within a few seconds either side of the current time
Add a short sleep before the assertion, so that the clocks have time to settle first
Inject a clock the test controls, or freeze time, so the expected value is known exactly
Let the CI server re-run the failed test automatically until it eventually passes

questions.explanation: A test that reads the real clock (or unseeded random numbers, or an unspecified ordering) has an input it cannot control, so it is non-deterministic. Control the input: pass in a clock, freeze time, seed the generator, sort before comparing. Margins, sleeps and automatic re-runs only hide the flakiness, and they teach the team to ignore failures.

questions.text: An integration test passes when it runs alone but fails when the whole suite runs, because it finds rows that another test left behind in the shared database. Which fix addresses the cause?

options.text: Give each test a clean start, such as a transaction rolled back after every test, or tables reset first
Run the failing test first in the suite, so that it sees the database before any other test has touched it
Add a sleep at the start of the failing test so the earlier tests have time to finish
Mark the test as flaky in CI, so that its failures no longer block the build

questions.explanation: A test that depends on what earlier tests left behind is coupled to them through the shared state, so its result depends on the order. Make every test start from a known state and leave nothing behind: roll back a per-test transaction, truncate tables, or build a fresh schema. Reordering, sleeping and ignoring failures hide the coupling instead of removing it.

questions.text: Service A calls service B's API, and A's tests use a mocked copy of B's responses. B's team renames a response field; both teams' CI stays green, but the integration breaks in production. What closes this gap without deploying both services together for every change?

options.text: More unit tests in A, written against the same mocked responses as before, to cover more cases
A contract test: A records what it relies on, and B's build verifies its real responses against that
A load test of B before every release, to see how it behaves with many concurrent callers
A stricter coverage target for B, so that every line of its response-building code is exercised by tests

questions.explanation: Each team tested against its own idea of the contract, and nothing ever compared the two. A consumer-driven contract test (for example with Pact) turns A's expectations into a check that runs in B's pipeline, so renaming the field fails B's build before release; more mock-based tests in A can never notice, because the mocks are frozen.

questions.text: Your service calls a payment API and must give up after 2 seconds. How can you test that behaviour without making the test wait?

options.text: Skip it, because timeouts can only be verified properly on a live production system
Call the real payment API from the test and hope that it happens to be slow enough to trigger the timeout
Use a test double that fails with a timeout at once, and assert how the service responds
Mock the service under test itself, so that the test finishes quickly and never waits

questions.explanation: Failure paths such as timeouts, 500 replies and malformed responses are exactly what production will hit, and a double can produce them instantly and repeatably. Waiting on a real dependency makes tests slow and random, and mocking the code under test means the test checks nothing about it.

questions.text: If a test suite reaches 100% line coverage, you can be sure the tests would catch a bug in any line.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Coverage only records which lines ran during the tests, not whether anything checked the results, so a test with no assertions still counts. It also cannot show code that is missing, such as validation nobody wrote, or inputs nobody tried; use it to find untested code, not as proof of quality.

questions.text: A property-based testing tool generates many inputs automatically and checks that a rule you state, such as decode(encode(x)) == x, holds for all of them, instead of relying on a few hand-picked examples.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: You describe a property that should always hold, and the tool tries hundreds of generated inputs, including awkward ones such as empty values, huge numbers and odd characters, then shrinks any failure to a small example. It complements example-based tests, which remain the clearest way to document specific behaviours.

tls-and-https-basics.title: TLS and HTTPS basics
tls-and-https-basics.description: What TLS does and does not protect, how certificates are checked, and where HTTPS ends in a real deployment.

questions.text: Which three guarantees does TLS give an HTTPS connection?

options.text: Compression, caching and load balancing
Encryption, integrity and server authentication
Authorization, rate limiting and logging
Anonymity, availability and data-at-rest protection

questions.explanation: TLS keeps the bytes unreadable to eavesdroppers, detects tampering, and proves the server is who its certificate says. It does not hide who you connected to and does not protect data once it is stored or after TLS ends.

questions.text: If a site presents a valid certificate and the browser shows a padlock, you can be sure the site is honest and safe.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The padlock means the connection is encrypted and the server is who its certificate says it is. A scam site can have a perfectly valid certificate for its own domain.

questions.text: When a client verifies a server's certificate during the TLS handshake, which checks does it make? Select all that apply.

options.text: The chain of signatures leads up to a root CA in its trust store
The hostname it asked for is covered by the certificate
The website's content has been reviewed and is safe
The current date is inside the certificate's validity period

questions.explanation: Chain of trust, hostname match and validity dates are what the client can actually check. Nothing in the certificate says anything about whether the site's content is safe.

questions.text: All your API clients suddenly fail with "certificate has expired". Which command shows the certificate's validity dates for a host?

options.text: curl -k https://example.com/
dig example.com TXT
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com, piped to openssl x509 -noout -dates
ss -tlnp on the client

questions.explanation: openssl s_client fetches the certificate and x509 -noout -dates prints notBefore and notAfter. curl -k would just skip verification and hide the problem, and the other commands inspect DNS or local sockets.

questions.text: A network observer between a client and an HTTPS site can typically still see which of these? Select all that apply.

options.text: The destination IP address
The value of the Authorization header
The JSON request body
The server name sent in the TLS handshake (SNI), in a typical setup

questions.explanation: TLS hides the HTTP content: headers, cookies, tokens and bodies. It does not hide the fact of the connection, so the IP address and normally the SNI hostname stay visible.

questions.text: TLS is terminated at your load balancer, and the app behind it sees plain http:// requests. How can the app learn that the client originally used HTTPS?

options.text: From an X-Forwarded-Proto header set by the proxy
From the port number on the app's own socket
From the TLS certificate in the request
It cannot be known, so apps must always redirect to HTTPS themselves

questions.explanation: The proxy adds the original scheme as X-Forwarded-Proto, which the app should trust only from a proxy it controls. The certificate and the original TLS session never reach the app once TLS has ended at the balancer.

questions.text: What does the header Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000 tell a browser?

options.text: The certificate will be renewed automatically in a year
Cookies should be encrypted at rest for a year
Session tokens expire after a year
For the next year, only connect to this site over HTTPS, even if the user types http://

questions.explanation: HSTS makes the browser refuse plain HTTP for the site, which defeats SSL-stripping downgrade attacks. It has nothing to do with certificate renewal or token lifetimes, and it only makes sense once HTTPS works everywhere on the site.

questions.text: Turning off certificate verification (curl -k, or verify=False in an HTTP library) in production code is acceptable because the traffic is still encrypted.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Without verification you no longer know who you are talking to, so a man-in-the-middle can present their own certificate and read everything. -k is for debugging a certificate problem only.

tokens-attention-transformers.title: Tokens, attention and transformers
tokens-attention-transformers.description: What a language model actually sees, and the attention mechanics inside a transformer: Q/K/V, scaling, masks and heads.

questions.text: What does a language model actually receive as input?

options.text: The raw characters of the text, one at a time
One ID per word, using a dictionary of every English word
Integer IDs of tokens, which are chunks of text from a fixed learned vocabulary
The text plus a separate list of its grammatical parts

questions.explanation: A tokenizer maps text to vocabulary entries, and the model only sees their integer IDs. A token can be a whole word, a word piece or a single character or byte, so it is not the same as a word.

questions.text: A sentence in Hindi or Japanese usually costs about the same number of tokens as the English sentence with the same meaning.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Tokenizers trained mostly on English text split non-Latin scripts into more, smaller tokens. The exact ratio depends on the language and the tokenizer (2-3 times is common, and it can be higher), but it is rarely close to 1. That raises both cost and latency for the same content.

questions.text: Why are queries, keys and values computed with three separate learned projections instead of using the token vectors X directly for all three?

options.text: It makes the matrices smaller so attention runs faster
Using X as both query and key makes the score matrix symmetric and biases each token toward attending to itself, so the model cannot learn directional relations between tokens
Softmax only works if the inputs come from a linear projection
It is needed to make the output the same length as the input

questions.explanation: If Q = K = X, the scores are X times X-transpose: the score from token i to token j always equals the score from j to i, and a token's dot product with itself (its squared length) tends to dominate its row, so each token is biased toward attending to itself. Separate Wq and Wk give each token a 'what I look for' vector and a different 'what I offer' vector, which removes the symmetry and lets the model learn which other tokens matter.

questions.text: Why are attention scores divided by sqrt(d_k) before the softmax?

options.text: Dot products grow with the dimension, so large scores would saturate the softmax and leave almost no gradient to learn from
It makes the weights for each row sum to exactly 1
It hides future tokens from the current position
It reduces the number of parameters in the layer

questions.explanation: The spread of dot products between random vectors scales with sqrt(d), so unscaled scores make softmax nearly one-hot and its gradient tiny. Softmax already normalises each row to 1, so that is not the reason for the scaling.

questions.text: A teammate implements a causal mask by setting the scores of future positions to 0 before the softmax. What goes wrong?

options.text: The model crashes with a shape error
Nothing; 0 and -inf give identical weights
Future positions get zero weight, but so do all past positions
Softmax still gives future positions a non-zero weight, so the model quietly leaks information from the future

questions.explanation: A score of 0 is not neutral to softmax; it counts as moderately plausible. Only adding -inf makes exp(-inf) = 0 and gives masked positions exactly zero weight. The bug does not crash, which is why it is dangerous.

questions.text: Going from 1 attention head to 8 heads at the same d_model adds roughly eight times as many parameters.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Wq, Wk, Wv and Wo stay d_model x d_model whatever the head count. The heads are made by splitting the projected vectors, so the parameter count is unchanged and each head just works in a smaller subspace with its own softmax.

questions.text: Which statements about sampling the next token are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Top-k keeps exactly k candidate tokens, whether the model is confident or torn
Top-p keeps fewer tokens when one token holds most of the probability mass
Temperature removes low-probability tokens from consideration
Greedy decoding samples tokens in proportion to their probabilities

questions.explanation: Top-k is a fixed count while top-p adapts to the shape of the distribution. Temperature only reshapes the probabilities and removes nothing, and greedy decoding always takes the single most likely token rather than sampling.

questions.text: A batch pads shorter sequences with [PAD] tokens so they fit in one tensor. Which are true of masking in this setup? Select all that apply.

options.text: A padding mask stops real tokens from attending to the padding
A padding mask and a causal mask are applied by different mechanisms, so they cannot be combined
Both kinds of mask work by adding -inf to scores before the softmax
A causal mask also hides padding that comes before the real tokens, so no padding mask is needed

questions.explanation: Padding masks and causal masks are the same additive -inf tool aimed at different problems: one hides non-content, the other hides the future. They are commonly combined additively before a single softmax. A causal mask hides only future positions: padding placed before the real tokens (left padding) is in their past and stays visible, and an encoder with bidirectional attention has no causal mask at all, so a padding mask is still needed.

transactions-and-isolation-levels.title: Transactions, isolation and locking
transactions-and-isolation-levels.description: Read anomalies, PostgreSQL's isolation levels, pessimistic and optimistic locking, and how to avoid deadlocks.

questions.text: What is PostgreSQL's default isolation level, and what does each statement see?

options.text: Serializable: every transaction runs as if alone
Repeatable Read: one snapshot for the whole transaction
Read Committed: each statement sees data committed before that statement began
Read Uncommitted: uncommitted changes are visible to everyone

questions.explanation: Read Committed prevents dirty reads but allows a later statement in the same transaction to see newly committed changes. The stronger levels must be requested explicitly.

questions.text: Inside one transaction you run SELECT ... WHERE status = 'open' twice. Between the runs another transaction inserts a matching row and commits, and your second run returns an extra row. Which anomaly is this?

options.text: Dirty read
Phantom read
Non-repeatable read
Lost update

questions.explanation: A phantom is a row appearing in (or vanishing from) a set matched by a predicate. A non-repeatable read is when an existing row you already read comes back with a different value. A dirty read involves uncommitted data.

questions.text: On PostgreSQL at Read Committed, an application that reads a balance, adds 10 in code and writes it back is safe from lost updates.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Two transactions can both read 100 and both write back their own result, so the second write overwrites the first. You need row locking, an atomic UPDATE, a version check, or a stronger isolation level with retries.

questions.text: Under PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ, two transactions update the same row. The first commits. What happens to the second?

options.text: It fails with a serialization error and must be retried
It silently overwrites the first update
It merges both updates automatically
It keeps waiting until the first transaction rolls back

questions.explanation: The second update blocks until the first finishes, then fails with 'could not serialize access due to concurrent update' because its snapshot is stale. The application has to catch that error and retry the whole transaction.

questions.text: Which approaches prevent a lost update when many requests change the same account balance? Select all that apply.

options.text: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE before computing the new balance
An UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND version = ? that is retried when it affects 0 rows
A single atomic statement such as UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 10
A plain SELECT then UPDATE at Read Committed, with a short transaction

questions.explanation: Pessimistic locking, optimistic versioning and an atomic update each stop two writers from acting on the same stale value. A short transaction narrows the window but does not close it.

questions.text: Two code paths transfer money between accounts A and B. One locks A then B, the other locks B then A, and they occasionally deadlock. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Raise deadlock_timeout so transactions wait longer
Switch both paths to Read Uncommitted
Add more connections to the pool
Have every code path lock the rows in the same order, such as lowest id first

questions.explanation: A deadlock needs a cycle of waits, and a consistent lock order makes a cycle impossible. A longer timeout only delays detection, and PostgreSQL has no real Read Uncommitted anyway.

questions.text: With optimistic locking, your UPDATE ... WHERE id = 'A' AND version = 7 reports 0 rows affected. What does that mean?

options.text: The row does not exist, so you should insert it
The database lost the update; you should restart the server
Someone else changed the row first, so re-read it and retry
The write succeeded but nothing needed changing

questions.explanation: The version no longer matches because another transaction bumped it. The application must detect the zero-row result, re-read the fresh row and retry (the re-read also shows if the row was deleted instead). This only pays off when conflicts are rare.

questions.text: Several workers poll a jobs table, and you want each worker to claim different rows without waiting on each other. Which clause fits?

options.text: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
SELECT ... FOR SHARE
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE with no other clause
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE

questions.explanation: SKIP LOCKED passes over rows another transaction already locked, so workers pick different rows. Plain FOR UPDATE makes every worker queue behind the first, and Serializable would produce errors to retry instead.

web-security-owasp-top-10.title: Web security and the OWASP Top 10
web-security-owasp-top-10.description: The most common ways web backends get broken into, and the habits that stop them.

questions.text: A logged-in customer changes the number in GET /api/invoices/1042 to 1043 and sees another customer's invoice. What is the proper fix?

options.text: Replace the numeric ids with random UUIDs so nobody can guess another invoice
Remove the links to other invoices from the page so users cannot find them
Check on the server that the caller owns the invoice, on every request
Serve the endpoint over HTTPS so that the id in the URL cannot be changed

questions.explanation: This is broken access control, here as an insecure direct object reference: logging in proves who the caller is, but the server must also check that this caller may see this object. Random ids only make guessing harder, and hiding links or adding HTTPS does nothing to stop someone who edits the URL.

questions.text: Which of these are safe ways to handle user input that ends up in a SQL query or a shell command?

options.text: Bind the search term as a parameter of a prepared statement
Strip quotes and semicolons from the requested sort column, then paste it into the SQL
Start the external program with its arguments as a list, without going through a shell
Reject any input that contains words such as DROP or SELECT
Map the requested sort name to a column from a fixed allowlist and refuse anything else

questions.explanation: Parameters keep values out of the SQL text, and an argument list keeps them out of a shell command line, so the input is never parsed as code. Table and column names cannot be bound as parameters, which is why an allowlist is used for them. Stripping characters or blocking keywords can be bypassed in ways you did not think of.

questions.text: An endpoint fetches a URL supplied by the user, for example to build a link preview. What is the best defence against server-side request forgery (SSRF)?

options.text: Allow only approved destinations and block private addresses after resolving DNS
Insist that the URL starts with https:// and that the host name looks like a public site
Reject any URL that contains the text localhost or 127.0.0.1, in any letter case
Apply a short timeout and a maximum response size to every outbound fetch

questions.explanation: In SSRF the attacker uses your server to reach places they cannot, such as internal services or the cloud metadata address. An https:// prefix does not stop that, text filters miss other spellings of the same address and host names that resolve to private ones, and timeouts only limit the load, so allow-list destinations and check the address the name resolves to.

questions.text: A production API returns a full stack trace, with file paths and the database host name, whenever a request fails. Why is that a security problem, and what is the fix?

options.text: It makes error responses slower, so debug mode only needs to go if latency becomes a problem
It breaks cross-origin rules in browsers, so add CORS headers to the error responses
It matters only on plain HTTP, so moving the whole site to HTTPS removes the risk
It reveals internals to attackers, so return a generic error and keep the details in logs

questions.explanation: Security misconfiguration includes debug output, default accounts, unneeded features and open storage buckets. A stack trace tells an attacker about your framework, versions, paths and queries, so return a generic message and keep the detail in your logs. Error pages have nothing to do with CORS, and HTTPS protects the connection, not what the server chooses to say.

questions.text: If the code your own team wrote has no vulnerabilities, a known security hole in a library you depend on, even an indirect one, cannot affect your service.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: A library runs inside your process with your service's privileges, so a hole in it, even in a dependency of a dependency, is a hole in your service. Keep a lockfile or software bill of materials, scan dependencies in CI and update promptly.

questions.text: Your login endpoint receives thousands of attempts from many different IP addresses, each trying one account with a password that appeared in an unrelated breach. A few succeed. Which defence fits best?

options.text: A slower, memory-hard hash for the passwords that are stored in your database
MFA, limits per account as well as per IP, and a breached-password check
Parameterised queries for the login lookup, so that usernames cannot carry SQL code
Longer random session ids, plus a brand new session id issued after every login

questions.explanation: This is credential stuffing: attackers replay username and password pairs leaked elsewhere and count on people reusing passwords, often from many IPs so that per-IP limits alone miss it. MFA, per-account throttling and breached-password checks all blunt it. Hashing, parameterised queries and session ids protect other things, not the live login.
