**The algorithm.** Walk the union of the node names once, treating a missing node as 0, and remember whether you ever saw `a` larger and whether you ever saw `b` larger. Neither is "equal", only `b` larger is "before", only `a` larger is "after", both is "concurrent". Do not compare the totals: `{"A": 5}` against `{"B": 6}` has the smaller sum but is concurrent.

**Merge** takes the position-wise maximum. That is the smallest clock that is after both inputs, and it is what a node does when a message arrives (before it also increments its own counter). Taking a maximum is why merging is commutative, associative and idempotent, which the next problem in this set, the G-Counter, builds on.

**Complexity.** O(n) in the number of nodes. In Dynamo-style stores, versions whose clocks compare as "concurrent" are kept side by side as siblings for the application to resolve.

wildcard-matching.title: Wildcard Matching
wildcard-matching.description: Match a whole string against a pattern with ? for one character and * for any run of characters.
wildcard-matching.statement:
A file-sync tool decides whether a file name matches a pattern such as `*.log` or `backup-??.tar`. Write `wildcard_match(text, pattern)` that returns `True` when the **whole** of `text` matches `pattern`:

- `?` matches exactly one character, any character.
- `*` matches any run of characters, including an empty one.
- Every other character matches only itself, case-sensitively (`[` and `]` are ordinary characters too).
- There is no escape syntax: a `*` or `?` inside `text` is an ordinary character, which a `?` or `*` in the pattern can match.

**Examples**

```python
wildcard_match("report.pdf", "*.pdf")              # True
wildcard_match("backup-07.tar", "backup-??.tar")   # True
wildcard_match("report.pdf", "*.txt")              # False
wildcard_match("", "***")                          # True, a star can match nothing
```

Trying every way to place the stars is exponential. Aim for O(len(text) · len(pattern)) or better.
hints: Try small cases by hand. `?` is easy. What makes `*` hard is that you do not know how many characters it should swallow. What are your choices when you meet one?

Think of pairs (position in the text, position in the pattern): the answer for one pair depends on a few neighbouring pairs, so you can fill a table. Or remember only the last star you saw, and whenever the match fails let that star swallow one more character and retry.

Never retry from scratch: placing every star in every possible way is exponential on `*a*a*a*a*b`. And check for `*` in the pattern before you compare characters, so that a `*` inside the text is not matched like an ordinary character.
wildcard-matching.explanation:
**The idea.** `?` is easy: it consumes one character. `*` is the hard part, because you do not know how many characters it should swallow. The key observation is that you never need to reconsider an *earlier* star once a later one has been placed: if the rest of the text can be matched at all, the earlier star could have swallowed less and left the work to the later one. So remember only the most recent star and where its match currently ends.

**The loop.** Walk both strings. On a `*` in the pattern, remember its position and the current text position, and first assume it matches nothing. On a matching character (or `?`), advance both. On a mismatch, if there was a star, let that star swallow one more character of the text and retry from just after it; with no star, the match has failed. When the text is used up, only stars may be left in the pattern.

**Why not try everything.** Placing every star in every possible way is exponential: `*a*a*a*a*b` against a long string of `a`s explores an astronomical number of combinations and finds none. The same blow-up hits a naive translation into a regular expression.

**Complexity.** O(len(text) · len(pattern)) in the worst case, usually close to linear, with O(1) extra space. The dynamic-programming alternative fills a table `match[i][j]`, "do the first i characters of the text match the first j characters of the pattern?", in O(n·m) time. Its recurrence is simple and it is easier to get right the first time.

**Usual mistakes.** Comparing characters before checking for `*` (a `*` inside the text would then be matched like an ordinary character), forgetting that trailing stars match the empty string, and reaching for `fnmatch`, which gives `[` and `]` a meaning of their own.

word-break.title: Word Break
word-break.description: Decide whether a string can be split into a sequence of words from a dictionary.
word-break.statement:
Return `True` if the string `s` can be built by joining words from `words` one after another, and `False` otherwise. A word may be used as many times as you like.

- The words must cover `s` exactly, in order, with nothing left over.
- The empty string can always be built (from zero words), even when `words` is empty: `word_break("", [])` is `True`.
- Words are not empty, and they may be prefixes of one another. Picking the longest (or the first) word that fits at each position is not always right.

**Examples**

```python
word_break("pineapplepie", ["pine", "apple", "pie", "pineapple"])   # True: pine + apple + pie
word_break("serverlogs", ["serve", "logs", "log"])                  # False
word_break("aaaa", ["a", "aaa"])                                    # True: words can be reused
```

Trying every way to cut the string is exponential, and the last test has 301 characters. Aim for roughly O(n²) or better, where n is the length of `s`.
tests: assert word_break("a" * 300 + "b", ["a" * length for length in range(1, 30)]) == False
hints: If you try every way to cut the string, the same ending gets examined again and again. Which yes/no question about a *prefix* of `s` could you answer once and reuse?
Let `splittable[i]` say whether the first `i` characters can be split into words. It is true when, for some `j < i`, `splittable[j]` is true and `s[j:i]` is a word. The empty prefix is splittable.
Look words up in a set, not a list. And do not commit to the longest (or the first) word that fits at a position: try every split point, because the greedy choice can strand the rest of the string.
word-break.explanation:
**The idea.** Let `splittable[i]` be True when the first `i` characters of `s` can be split into words. The empty prefix is splittable (`splittable[0]` is True). A longer prefix is splittable when some earlier split point `j` has `splittable[j]` True and the piece `s[j:i]` is a word. The answer is `splittable[len(s)]`.

**Why not try every split.** Every position can end a word or not, so the number of ways to cut grows exponentially (300 letters `a` with the words `a`, `aa`, `aaa`, ... have astronomically many). The table answers each prefix once and reuses it.

**Details.** Keep the words in a set so a lookup is O(1) instead of a scan of a list. A piece longer than the longest word can never match, so `start` only has to look back that far; that turns O(n²) pieces into O(n · longest word). Greedy rules fail: with `ab`, `abc` and `cd`, taking the longest word at the start of `abcd` strands the `d`.

**Follow-up.** To return one actual split, or all of them, remember for each end position which start worked and walk back; to count the splits, add up instead of stopping at the first success.

word-ladder.title: Word Ladder
word-ladder.description: Find the shortest chain of one-letter word changes from one word to another, using words from a list.
word-ladder.statement:
Write `word_ladder(begin_word, end_word, word_list)`, which returns the number of words in the **shortest** transformation sequence from `begin_word` to `end_word`, or `0` if there is none.

- Each step changes exactly one letter, and every word after the first must be in `word_list`. `begin_word` does not have to be in the list.
- The length counts both ends: `cat -> cot` has length 2.
- All words are lower case and have the same length, and `begin_word` and `end_word` are different.
- If `end_word` is not in `word_list`, the answer is `0`.
- The list can hold thousands of words.

**Examples**

```python
word_ladder("cold", "warm", ["cord", "card", "ward", "warm", "worm"])   # 5: cold, cord, card, ward, warm
word_ladder("cat", "cot", ["cot"])                                      # 2
word_ladder("cold", "warm", ["cord", "card", "ward"])                   # 0, "warm" is not in the list
```

Comparing every word with every other word is too slow for a long list.
tests: dictionary = ["".join("abcdefghi"[(n // 9 ** k) % 9] for k in range(4)) for n in range(9 ** 4)]
cut_off = [w for w in dictionary if sum(a != b for a, b in zip(w, "iiii")) != 1]
hints: Think of each word as a node, with an edge between two words that differ in one letter. What does "shortest transformation" mean on that graph, and which search finds it?

A breadth-first search from `begin_word` finds the shortest path; the first time you reach `end_word` is the answer. The costly part is finding a word's neighbors: comparing it with every other word is O(N).

Find neighbors without comparing all pairs: group the words by pattern (`c*ld`, `co*d`, ...) in a dictionary, or try all 26 letters at each position and look the result up in a set. Mark words as seen when you queue them, and remember the answer counts words, not steps.
word-ladder.explanation:
**The idea.** Think of every word as a node and join two words when they differ in exactly one letter. A shortest transformation is then a shortest path in an unweighted graph, which breadth-first search finds: it explores all words one change away, then two changes away, and so on, so the first time it reaches `end_word` the number of words on the way is the shortest. Mark a word as seen when you queue it, so nothing is queued twice.

**The expensive part is finding neighbors.** Comparing a word with every other word costs O(N) per word, O(N²) overall, too slow for thousands of words. Two faster ways: group the words by pattern (`c*ld`, `co*d`, `col*`, ...) in a dictionary, so the neighbors of a word are the other members of its groups; or try every letter in every position and look the result up in a set. Both cost O(length) lookups per word instead of O(N).

**Counting.** The answer counts words, not steps, so `cat -> cot` is 2. Words missing from the list are not allowed, and neither is an `end_word` that is not in it.

**Complexity.** About O(N × L²) time with the pattern groups (L is the word length, because building each pattern costs O(L)). Follow-up: a *bidirectional* search, from both ends at once, explores far fewer words on a big list; and returning the ladder itself, or all shortest ladders, needs the parent of each word.

zero-one-knapsack.title: 0/1 Knapsack
zero-one-knapsack.description: Choose items, each at most once, to get the most value into a bag with a weight limit.
zero-one-knapsack.statement:
You have items with the given `weights` and `values` (item `i` weighs `weights[i]` and is worth `values[i]`) and a bag that holds a total weight of at most `capacity`. Return the largest total value you can carry. Each item can be taken at most once, which is the "0/1" in the name.

- Weights are whole numbers of at least 1; values and `capacity` are whole numbers of at least 0.
- With no items, or a `capacity` of `0`, the answer is `0`. An item heavier than the whole bag can never be taken.
- Return only the best total value, not which items give it.

**Examples**

```python
knapsack([1, 3, 4, 5], [1, 4, 5, 7], 7)      # 9    (the items of weight 3 and 4)
knapsack([10, 20, 30], [60, 100, 120], 50)   # 220  (the items of weight 20 and 30)
knapsack([2], [9], 10)                       # 9    (the one item, taken once)
```

Trying every subset of items takes exponential time, and the tests have 40 items. Aim for O(items × capacity).
tests:
import random
def brute_force(weights, values, capacity, i=0):
    if i == len(weights):
        return 0
    best = brute_force(weights, values, capacity, i + 1)                    # leave item i
    if weights[i] <= capacity:                                               # or take it
        best = max(best, values[i] + brute_force(weights, values, capacity - weights[i], i + 1))
    return best
rng = random.Random(5)
random_bags = []
for _ in range(200):
    count = rng.randint(0, 8)
    random_bags.append(([rng.randint(1, 6) for _ in range(count)], [rng.randint(0, 9) for _ in range(count)], rng.randint(0, 15)))
def wrong_on(bags):
    wrong = []
    for weights, values, capacity in bags:
        got = knapsack(list(weights), list(values), capacity)
        want = brute_force(weights, values, capacity)
        if got != want:
            wrong.append(f"knapsack({weights}, {values}, {capacity}) returned {got}, expected {want}")
    return wrong[:3]
hints: For each item there are only two choices: leave it or take it. Which two numbers describe where you are after deciding about the first few items?
Let `best[c]` be the most value that fits in capacity `c` using the items seen so far. For an item of weight `w` and value `v`: `best[c] = max(best[c], best[c - w] + v)`.
Update the capacities from high to low. Going upwards lets the same item be counted again in the same pass.
zero-one-knapsack.explanation:
**The idea.** Go through the items one at a time and keep `best[c]`, the most value that fits in capacity `c` using the items looked at so far. For a new item of weight `w` and value `v`, every capacity `c >= w` has two options: leave the item (`best[c]` stays as it is) or take it, which leaves `c - w` for the earlier items: `best[c - w] + v`. Keep the larger.

**The detail that makes it 0/1.** Loop the capacity from high to low. Then `best[c - w]` still holds the answer *without* the current item. Looping upwards would let the same item be added again in the same pass, which is the unbounded knapsack, where every item may be taken any number of times.

**Complexity.** O(items × capacity) time and O(capacity) space. That is *pseudo-polynomial*: polynomial in the value of the capacity, not in the number of digits needed to write it, and the general problem is still NP-hard. The same table answers "does some subset add up to X?" and "can this list be split into two equal halves?".
